We investigate the orbital stability of solitary anharmonic oscillators in a one-dimensional system without any external influences, relying on the full spectrum approach. This involves examining the behavior of a general two-parameter family of Hamiltonian Schr\"{o}dinger operators and its relationship to a specific anharmonic oscillator model. By analyzing the properties of this model, we can determine conditions that ensure the stability of its solitary waves. Our investigation reveals that these conditions cannot be met for a specific anharmonic oscillator when it is coupled to a massless scalar field in its vacuum state. However, we find that its solitary waves remain orbitally stable when coupled to a massive scalar field with a specific range of parameter values. This is in contrast to the harmonic oscillator case, where its solitary waves lose their shape over time when coupled to a massless scalar field, yet remain stable when coupled to a massive scalar field with a certain range of parameter values. Our research also explores the relationship between the anharmonic oscillator's frequency and its coupling to the scalar field, demonstrating that the minimum number of quanta required for stability increases with the anharmonic contribution, but can be lower if the mass of the scalar field exceeds its critical value. Our stability criteria are based on the properties of the discrete spectrum of the Hamiltonian Schr\"{o}dinger operators and provide a foundation for investigating more complex systems that incorporate this anharmonic oscillator model. Systematic investigation of these systems will be addressed in subsequent research projects. Our research projects also involve developing numerical methods to investigate the stability of solitary waves in these systems. Our results for the anharmonic oscillator case were verified by directly integrating the Schr\"{o}dinger equation numerically. Our research projects aim to investigate the orbital stability of solitary waves in a range of one-dimensional systems that incorporate the anharmonic oscillator model, specifically focusing on systems that include a particle coupled to a massive scalar field, a FPU chain with isolated solitary waves, and variable period chains with isolated solitary waves. Our research projects also involve exploring the relationship between the drivers of instability in the harmonic oscillator case and the properties of the scalar field. Our research projects provide a foundation for investigating the stability of moving solitary waves and systems with periodic boundaries, which is a natural extension of our research. We demonstrate that a distinctly characterized subset of highly unraveled, finite field extensions of the rational numbers Q contains all possible instances of low-degree, non-abelian extensions with complex ramification. This subset is comprised of subfields of a particular type of transcendental extension generated from the 72nd root of unity, specifically those with a Galois group possessing a specific structure when mapped to the symmetric group S_{72}. Furthermore, our findings involve an in-depth analysis of the additive Galois module associated with these extensions, revealing a connection to the Milnor K_2 functor via the Suslin-Voevodsky construction, as well as connections to the absolute Galois group, local fields, and the arithmetic of number fields. These results also imply the non-existence of certain polynomial equations over the integers Z with specific properties, namely those defined by a particular family of forms with a particular factorization property. These findings expand upon prior work of the second author, contributing to the characterization of highly unraveled finite field extensions of the rational numbers Q, while also exploring connections to the absolute Galois group, local fields, the arithmetic of number fields, the 72nd root of unity, and the non-existence of specific polynomial equations over the integers Z. Systematic methods for constructing and analyzing these subfields can be found in the accompanying thesis of the second author. This research was inspired by the problems presented in the work of Harborth, Harborth-Kuhlier, and Schiermeyer. The relationship between the additive Galois module associated with these extensions and the Milnor K_2 functor was discovered through the study of local K_2 functors as described in the thesis of the third author. The connection to the arithmetic of number fields, specifically related to the Riemann hypothesis and the distribution of prime ideals in number fields, was explored by the second author in collaboration with Michael Spiegler. The third author also investigated the possibility of constructing similar results for higher-degree, non-abelian extensions with complex ramification in his thesis. To identify a neutral long-lived particle (NLP) at a collider, researchers consider various factors such as NLP decay length, production process, and relevant detectors. A comprehensive analysis across various NLP searches indicates that for a neutral scalar NLP with a mass of one TeV and a lifetime measured in microseconds, the most effective search strategy at current colliders involves examining for displaced signatures in the missing transverse momentum channel using the ATLAS detector. A mark-one TeV neutral vector NLP with a similar lifetime is more difficult to detect, and the most promising approach at present colliders is to look for signatures of a long-lived neutral vector NVL in the with-leptons final state using the ATLAS or CMS detector. A study of neutral heavy gauges NLP shows that such particles are challenging to detect at current colliders, primarily due to their weak interactions, and the most promising search for a one TeV neutral heavy gauge NLP with a lifetime in the order of microseconds involves examining for displaced leptons in missing transverse momentum events using the ATLAS or CMS detector. A comprehensive analysis across various NLP searches also highlights that for a neutral NLP with a mass of one TeV and a lifetime measured in microseconds, the most effective search strategy at future colliders involves examining for displaced signatures in the missing transverse momentum channel using the ATLAS or HL-ATLAS detector, regardless of NLP type. A mark-one TeV neutral vector NLP with a similar lifetime is more difficult to detect at future colliders, and the most promising approach is to look for signatures of a long-lived neutral vector NVL in the with-leptons final state using the ATLAS or HL-ATLAS detector. Ultimately, the most challenging NLP to detect at future colliders is the neutral heavy gauges NLP due to its weak interactions, and the most promising search for a one TeV neutral heavy gauge NLP with a lifetime in the order of microseconds involves examining for displaced leptons in missing transverse momentum events using the ATLAS or HL-ATLAS detector. A study of neutral long-lived gluons NLP across various production processes indicates that such particles are challenging to detect at current colliders, primarily due to their strong interactions with a minimal energy output in semi-leptonic final states, and the most promising search for a one TeV neutral long-lived gluons NLP with a lifetime in the order of microseconds involves examining for displaced semi-leptonic events using the ATLAS or CMS detector

Understanding how word meanings change over time requires accounting for changes in contextual information, as these can influence the magnitude of semantic shifts. This study investigates the impact of contextual variance, as measured by word embedding dispersion, on the semantic evolution of time-sensitive words. Our analysis reveals that considering the temporal context is essential for accurately capturing the development of these words' meanings. Furthermore, our results show that contextual variance can affect the direction of semantic shift, with words experiencing increased contextual variance in some cases and decreased in others, and these patterns hold across multiple embedding models. Our findings also demonstrate the limitations of static embeddings in capturing the temporal evolution of words with fluctuating contextual variance, and our proposed method, TempCo, is shown to effectively track the development of these words more accurately than previous approaches. Our study highlights the significance of contextual variance in informing the design of future methods aimed at better understanding the temporal evolution of word meanings. Researchers have used radio-frequency sensitive detectors placed near tokamak plasma to discover novel constraints on ultra-light dark matter, specifically for a model where a scalar field affects the behavior of neutral particles. By analyzing how particles interact with the tokamak's magnetic field, a lower limit was placed on the mass of these particles at 1.45 times 10 to the power of negative 20 Hortons, or 1.45 E20 Hortons. This limit applies under an assumption of efficient dark matter distribution and normal neutrino behavior, and it holds for a wide range of particle frequencies interacting with the tokamak device known as MAST. This discovery paves the way for tightened limits through further experimentation with larger tokamaks like JET and ST1600, and it highlights the dark matter detection potential of existing experimental data from the JET and LHD devices. This finding also presents a distinguished phase in the behavior of neutral particles that could have implications for their influence on the formation and evolution of the universe. This research constrains the range of particle frequencies that may influence the behavior of neutral particles, offering a basis for a new field of study called "neutraseismology." This exploration can be expanded by analyzing plasma interactions with solid walls in the tokamak, and it may yield even more stringent limits on ultra-light dark matter. This study's restrictions apply specifically to particles with masses between 10 to the power of negative 20 and 10 to the power of negative 12 Hortons, and it imposes a minimum on the interaction strength between these particles and neutral particles at or below 10 to the power of negative 5. This discovery was made by analyzing the behavior of neutral particles in the tokamak's edge plasma, and it demonstrates the feasibility of a new experimental approach that can provide a comprehensive understanding of ultra-light dark matter. Understanding how retinal cell types are generated, move, and position themselves is crucial for comprehending retinal development. In this study, we used high-resolution imaging and nuclear labeling to observe the dynamics of retinal nuclear migration in zebrafish. Our findings reveal the retinal nuclei's initial random movement gives way to a highly organized, centripetal distribution, driven by the slow contraction of a broad, retinal-wide wave-like pattern. This process, which we call the "retinal roll-up," is controlled by the slow movement of a small group of pioneer cells. Our data also show that cells within a specific retinal layer move independently, migrating towards a retinal "pole" before slowing and differentiating into a specific cell type. Our research reveals the intricate mechanics underlying nuclear migration and layer formation during retinal development, and demonstrates how a simple mechanical process, driven by a small group of pioneer cells, generates the complex retinal architecture seen in adult animals. Our results further highlight the widespread occurrence of wave-like patterns in developmental biology, and suggest that a unified understanding of the underlying mechanical principles is necessary for a complete comprehension of these processes. Our study's findings have been publicly available since 2019 at the related website.

Reconstructing images from measurements is crucial in various tasks, including image reconstruction, deblurring, and decompressive sensing. We address the critical issue of reducing mutual coherence in the sensing matrix, which significantly impacts recovery performance, given its direct relationship with the minimum number of measurements required. To circumvent the NP-hard nature of mutual coherence minimization, we propose a novel optimization routine that leverages the $l_0$ norm and exploits the sparsity of natural images. Utilizing the tight connection between the $l_0$ norm and the number of non-zero elements, we develop a non-convex optimization problem that can be solved effectively, yielding a convex program with an analytic solution. To improve recovery performance, we introduce a sensing matrix design framework based on the projected gradient descent method, which meets the required constraint of mutual coherence. Comprehensive simulations, including a real-world application (i.e., reconstructing compressed MRI images), demonstrate substantial improvements in recovery error, PSNR, and SSIM values, when compared to standard techniques. Specifically, our approach shows significant gains at moderate compression ratios, e.g., reducing the minimum required measurements from 1.5 to 1 during MRI reconstruction. We also theoretically analyze the connection between the proposed matrix design and mutual coherence, which provides a compressed sensing perspective on image reconstruction. To facilitate widespread adoption, we have made our proposed code public, along with example datasets, to enable easy integration into various research settings. Resources can be accessed via the following link: https://github.com/AliHassanX/MatrixDesignForImageReconstruction. To differentiate our contribution from compressed sensing, we refer to image reconstruction as deimaging. To emphasize the wide applicability of deimaging, we will use this term interchangeably with image reconstruction in the subsequent text. To illustrate the practical value of deimaging, we will demonstrate its efficacy using MRI reconstruction as a representative example. To this end, we will utilize the highly acclaimed SPIP software, coupled with realistic simulation environments, to provide realistic deimaging test data. To leverage the inherent sparsity of natural images, we will employ the $l_0$ norm-based matrix design framework, which will serve as a fundamental component for developing various inverse problems solutions. To validate the effectiveness and wide applicability of our proposed method, we will conduct comprehensive simulations, including MRI deimaging, which will be used as a representative real-world case study. We investigate the scaling behavior of active systems at various dimensions, specifically 2D to 5D, using the linearized hydrodynamic model. Our analysis shows that these systems exhibit unique scaling characteristics that diverge from conventional hydrodynamic principles in lower dimensions. Particularly, in 2D, we find that the viscosity and the speed of sound become infinite, whereas the mean squared displacement of individual particles displays a Kardar-Paris-Shepard-like scaling, albeit with a modified exponent. Our findings can be experimentally verified using vibrated granular media and have previously been observed in computer simulations of active matter. Additionally, the infinite viscosity dimension implies that the Knudsen scaling will prevail in these systems. Our theoretical approach also yields the speed of sound and the mean squared displacement as specific fractions of fundamental units in 2D and 3D. Furthermore, our model predicts the existence of a upper limit for the Peclet number in these systems. Our research paves the way for a deeper comprehension of active matter dynamics and highlights the significance of dimensionality on the underlying hydrodynamic principles. Our linearized hydrodynamic model can be applied to various active systems, including the ones mentioned above, and provides a straightforward, mathematical framework for the study of their scaling behavior. We conducted a text extraction project centered on Sri Lankan ID cards, aiming to apply machine learning in an supervised setting to achieve 100% accuracy.  To begin, we developed a program to automatically collect relevant images and train a model to accurately extract information from these images.  The accuracy of our machine learning model was monitored at each stage of development.  Our findings show that the integration of NLP enhances our results by increasing the model's accuracy to 94% in a supervised setting from 82% without the use of NLP techniques.  The model's performance was evaluated using precision, recall, and F1 score metrics.  Our approach can be applied to similar projects involving the extraction of information from scanned documents.  Our code is available online for the benefit of other researchers working on similar projects.  In the process, we encountered several challenges, including the degradation of machine learning model performance when dealing with low quality images, a problem that future researchers may also encounter and can be addressed by implementing techniques such as image enhancement.  Our work was conducted in Python 3, utilizing the OpenCV library for image processing, the PyTesseract library for text extraction, the NLTK library for text preprocessing, and the scikit-learn library for machine learning.  Our code can be accessed from https://github.com/TharikaID/text-extraction-from-nid-card. Quantum systems driven by periodic forces can exhibit fascinating behavior, and studying these systems requires a combination of mathematical techniques from both physics and engineering. Within the framework of classical mechanics, driven systems can be effectively analyzed using coherent states, which represent physical observables and can be used to develop efficient numerical methods for solving various problems, including stochastic dynamics and quantum transport. Building upon this foundation, this article extends the use of coherent states to a range of quantum mechanics applications, including time-dependent Schrödinger equations, stochastic equations, and quantum transport equations. We demonstrate the accuracy and computational efficiency of these methods by applying them to driven quantum systems in both periodic and stochastic environments. [Published in]{Bogdan et al. Using archival radio observations from the VLA, we have discovered three small, rapidly spinning asteroids that are orbiting the Sun between the orbits of Earth and Mars.  These objects, known as asteroid comets or main belt comets, are thought to originate from the main asteroid belt and produce comet-like tails when their highly accelerated spin causes them to shed small particles.  We detected three such asteroids, designated 1986 UA (spin period 275.8 days), 2009 WJ51 (spin period 77.8 days with accelerated spin), and 2016 VA$_{64}$ (spin period 178.7 days with accelerated spin).  Two of these results were previously unknown, while the first detection of 1986 UA was made in the past.  To confirm its classification as an asteroid comet, the spin period of 1986 UA had to be verified, while additional evidence for the comet-like behavior of 2009 WJ$_{51}$ and 2016 VA$_{64}$ was found.  Future targeted radio observations at the VLA or similar telescopes during the predicted perihelion passages of these asteroids may reveal further evidence of their comet-like activity.  Additionally, high-resolution optical imaging or high-speed photometry of these objects may provide additional information about their spin periods, orbital elements, and the origin of their highly accelerated spin.  It is worth noting that the spin period of 1986 UA, with a period of approximately 276 days, is closely matched to half of its orbital period around the Sun, a phenomenon known as spin-orbit resonance.  This type of resonance may explain the accelerated spin of this asteroid.  However, more data is needed to confirm this hypothesis for the other detected asteroids. A persistent challenge in machine learning applies to systems that exhibit complex behaviors on various time scales, where traditional techniques struggle to accurately predict long-term dynamics. In a study involving a prominent example - the complex Ginzburg-Landau equation with periodic forcing and multiple coexisting states of oscillatory and stationary behaviors - our innovative reservoir computing method effectively handles a wide range of time frames, up to 100 times greater than the initial period, with high precision near the edge of the parameter space conducive to learning, surpassing the limitations of conventional techniques by 10 times. Our approach, successfully modeling multiple coexisting states and accurately predicting both short-term and long-term dynamics with high precision, demonstrates a promising future for overcoming the constraints of time scale in machine learning. Our approach is open-source and available for public use.

This approach enables the state transition matrix to be computed while minimizing the impact of model errors. As a result, the state transition matrix is guaranteed to be approximately equivalent to the original system's state transition matrix over a predetermined time frame, thus estimating the reachable state set within a specified time frame. This analysis is performed through the solution of a system of nonlinear equations, which can be effectively solved using numerical methods. Moreover, our analysis is implemented using a discrete-time version of the inverse optimal feedback design, and this implementation is computationally efficient due to the use of a specialized structure that enables the state transition matrix to be accurately approximated via a series expansion. This results in a computationally lighter solution compared to other methods, making it suitable for modern embedded systems. Our approach is further enhanced by integrating the reachable state set analysis with $\mathcal{L}_1$ tube methods, which provides a practical solution for large-scale systems. This integrated solution reduces the required memory and computational resources, making it applicable to complex systems of high dimensional states and control inputs. We demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our method by applying it to a representative aircraft system and comparing it with alternative methods. This comparison highlights the computational benefits and accuracy improvements offered by our approach, particularly when analyzing systems with high-dimensional states and control inputs. Our methodology is versatile and can be adapted for analyzing system performance, safety, and reliability in various applications, including autonomous system design, motion planning, and control system validation. The distinction between living and non-living entities is fundamental to how we organize our surroundings, yet this categorization can be subjective and vary greatly across cultures, as seen in examples like the classification of vampires as living or dead. Drawing on these observations, our research proposes a theory that the concept of animacy comprises two distinct aspects: visual categorizability and agency. Visual categorizability refers to the ease with which we can identify something as being of a specific visual category, whereas agency represents the perceived capacity for an entity to act independently. By separating these components, our study reveals that they contribute independently to the complexity of the animacy spectrum. For example, we can observe that animals are generally considered to be animate due to their visible characteristics, whereas ghosts are animate because of their exhibited behavior. By separating these aspects, our research provides a more nuanced understanding of the animacy continuum and highlights the distinct roles that visual recognition and agency play in defining the boundaries between life and death, as well as those between different types of living things. Miller and Shahidi initially proposed that there are an infinite number of zeros lying outside the critical line 1/2 in favor of Landau-Siegel zeros. However, Conjecture 3.3 from their work suggests that, in contrast, all non-trivial zeros of automorphic L-functions should remain within the critical line 1/2, given certain conditions. This paper explores the relationship between zero repulsion and the condition that there are only finitely many zeros at the critical line, building upon the work of Miller and Shahidi. Specifically, it is demonstrated that the absence of zeros on the critical line 1/2 is equivalent to zero repulsion occurring for an infinite number of Dirichlet L-functions that are induced from automorphic ones. Moreover, this result can be applied to establish the existence of zeros on the critical line 1/2 for a subclass of GL_2 automorphic L-functions, where zero repulsion is observed for only those with an infinite number of zeros. Finally, this phenomenon is further examined to understand its relationship with Siegel zeros and the classification of automorphic representations into inner and orthogonal components. This research extends the principles of quantum relational Hoare logic to accommodate programs with approximate output relationships, utilizing a concept called "perspective" that compares the actual output with the desired output. To facilitate this, a new form of relational assertion is introduced, effectively linking a program's behavior to any desired output relation, even an imperfect one. Building upon this, our development of quantum relational Hoare triples is capable of handling programs whose input-output relationships can be quantitatively assessed, leveraging a mechanism to handle "fuzziness" while maintaining the integrity of quantum properties. Key contributions of this work include developing a methodology to derive quantitative relational assertions from FuzzZ, a formal language describing these relationships, as well as creating an verification tool that can validate the behavior of programs with respect to these assertions. A set of examples, encompassing both mathematical functions and real-world implementations, demonstrate the applicability and efficacy of our framework. Ultimately, this research aims to bridge the gap between verifiable and practical programs by providing a framework for the development of reliable and accurate programs within the quantum realm. This work is relevant to a variety of applications, including secure multi-party computation, contract theory, and economic design, all of which necessitate trustworthy program behavior based on input-output relationships. By extending the principles of quantum relational Hoare logic, this research opens up possibilities for refining program specifications, developing new verification methods, and creating trustworthy quantum software. This development also offers insights into defining quantum relational Hoare triples and verifying programs with respect to approximate output relationships, demonstrating the value of a quantum formalism in addressing challenges unique to quantum computing, while offering a complementary perspective to classical formalisms. This research has been publicly available since the paper's initial publication on arXiv in 2021. Since then, the associated verification tool has undergone significant enhancements, with the most recent update occurring in March 2023, when the project was transferred to the GitHub platform under the name QHOL. This updated version features various improvements, including a more efficient verification process, the ability to handle approximate output relationships, and a user-friendly interface for defining program specifications and verifying program behavior. This project is currently being actively developed by a team of researchers, with plans to enhance the QHOL verifier further, expand the set of predefined predicates, and create instructional materials for users. Recent super-spreader events in enclosed settings have highlighted the significance of tail events within epidemiological frameworks. To better understand these events, we integrate a super-spreader distribution, specifically the power-law, into a compartmental model, refining the standard SEIR model for enclosed environments. Our hybrid model, with a detailed mass transport description, accurately captures rapid transmission and shows that a small fraction of highly infectious individuals can drive infection dynamics. By analyzing this model, we find that the peak infected fraction occurs shortly after initial exposure and that a small group of highly infectious individuals can cause outbreaks in vaccine-only scenarios. Furthermore, our model predicts distinct epidemic trajectory phases, supported by numerical simulations, and provides explicit power-law exponents governing these phases, offering a clear understanding of the underlying dynamics. Our hybrid model serves as a foundational framework for exploring policy interventions and analyzing real-world data. Our research demonstrates the pivotal role that super-spreader distribution dynamics play in shaping the course of epidemics within enclosed settings. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/CompDynamicsGroup/power_law_seir. Our hybrid model has been published in the journal Physics Review E, volume 99, issue 4, 2029 (2029). Our study was featured in the news outlet Science Daily (2029). To enhance the precision of magnetic field modeling, we're introducing a revised model that takes into account the fill fraction of magnetic features, in addition to their strength and location. This improvement is particularly beneficial in computationally expensive simulations, such as lattice QCD simulations, where Monte Carlo samples are extensively utilized, thereby significantly benefiting from our optimized unit. Leveraging the MCC unit, our research presents a specific implementation of complex-valued affine coupling layers that significantly reduce computational costs by approximately an order of magnitude compared to conventional methods, with minimal effects on statistical precision, as validated through lattice Landau gauge simulations involving vector fields. Numerous machine learning tasks require private datasets to be shared and collaborative work to be done, yet traditional methods like grid search are impractical due to the need to keep the data private. This motivates the development of a novel, collaborative hyperparameter optimization approach, specifically designed for the likes of decentralized finance and research collaborations, where data cannot be exchanged. This new method, a decentralized hyperparameter optimization approach based on reinforcement learning, enables multiple parties to jointly find optimal hyperparameters for a central task without revealing their individual datasets. In the process, each participant generates private, task-specific features from a centralized, publicly accessible dataset, and contributes a centralized, pseudo-dataset to a decentralized environment. Within this environment, a shared, learning agent develops policies to evaluate the pseudo-datasets and identify the most suitable hyperparameters, which are in turn used to train a student agent for each participant. These student agents are then decentralized models that utilize the learned hyperparameters to optimize the central task on their individual private datasets. Evaluations using multiple datasets confirm the effectiveness and efficiency of this approach, as it outperforms non-decentralized hyperparameter optimization for various tasks, including text classification, sentiment analysis, and machine translation, without compromising data privacy. Experimental parameters are also provided for easy replication, and the associated code has been made available online.

Using a larger dataset of 107 distant planetary nebulae, the Fornax cluster's distance has been recalculated to be 4.88 plus or minus 0.04 megaparsecs. This revised measurement is based on the planetary nebulae luminosity function and supersedes a previous estimate of the cluster's distance made with a smaller planetary nebula sample. Additionally, the new analysis includes 13 planetary nebulae that were previously excluded due to uncertainty about the cluster's distance. These 13 planetary nebulae were initially considered too distant to be members of the Fornax cluster but are now incorporated into the revised calculation. LifeStream is a cutting-edge, automated optimization framework aimed at accelerating numerical science workloads through a unique, four-stage process: it generates test data to simulate real-world inputs, compiles numerical computations using popular scientific programming languages, runs benchmarking tests to identify performance-critical code, and refines the code using a combination of numerical transformation techniques and metaprogramming tools to achieve maximum speed efficiency. LifeStream's efficacy was demonstrated across five distinct scientific domains, processing real-world datasets of varying sizes, and it consistently delivered superior results when compared to hand-optimized numerical libraries, showcasing the effectiveness of its optimization strategy. Furthermore, LifeStream's source code has been made available on public repositories for community feedback and future development. We explore various spaces in 3D where a specific type of curve, known as a Bertrand curve, is well-defined and analyze its characteristics. Bertrand curves connect two given lines with the same direction and define a curve whose normal passes through a fixed point. We examine hyperbolic Bertrand curves in spaces with constant curvature, specifically in Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic contexts. By formulating these curves as differential equations, we derive their distinct forms based on the type of space. Furthermore, we identify specific conditions under which a Bertrand curve exists in these spaces and analyze its characteristics. In the Euclidean case, a spherical Bertrand curve is shown to be a circle, while its hyperbolic counterpart is an equidistant curve. Additionally, we discuss questions related to curve classification and uniqueness. Moreover, we provide graphical representations of Euclidean and hyperbolic Bertrand curves. Lastly, we discuss their geodesic properties and possible generalizations.

We investigate how loss function selection influences the performance of adversarial natural language inference, a task that requires generating sentences that are either true or false based on input text. Adversarial NLI can be solved using various loss functions, but our analysis reveals that optimizing KL Divergence yields superior results when attempting to mislead LSTMs and compares favorably to other loss functions when using Transformers. By analyzing individual component scores, we found that loss function has a more significant impact than hyperparameter tuning for LSTMs. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrated that KL Divergence enables the generation of highly accurate adversarial sentences, with up to 85% accuracy in predicting the sentence's label, in contrast to 60% when using cross-entropy loss. Our findings also reveal that loss function influences the distribution of generated sentences, with KL Divergence prioritizing sentences that are more confidently labeled as false. Our Adversarial NLI code is available online. By exploring loss function effects, our research intends to encourage examination of optimization objectives in adversarial training and similar generative tasks. Knowing the optimal loss function can depend on task components, our experiments provide a foundation for similar Adversarial NLI tasks, and our code enables replication and expansion upon existing models. Our research demonstrates the significance of loss function in Adversarial NLI, offering a starting point for related tasks and providing actionable guidance for future Adversarial NLI research. This research develops a computational approach to simulate the thermomechanical properties of polymers as they undergo crystallization under deformation. By applying thermodynamic principles, viscoelastic material models are combined with kinetics equations that account for crystallization, resulting in a multi-scale, multi-field formulation. This formulation includes temperature, crystallinity, molecular weight, and stress fields. It is implemented using a numerical method that solves for the rates of change of temperature, crystallinity, and molecular weight. Stress is derived from equilibrium equations. This approach assumes that molecular weight changes in a way that maintains material consistency and is influenced by temperature, crystallinity, and strain. The development is applied to model stress-strain curves observed during uniaxial tension tests on polyethylene samples. These models can be further refined by adjusting their kinetic parameters. This research focuses on thermomechanical properties of polyethylene but the proposed methodology can be adapted to study other polymers that exhibit strain-induced crystallization behavior. The developed code is capable of handling two-dimensional problems as well as three-dimensional problems. The validation against experimental data shows good agreement. The code can be utilized to investigate other phenomena such as material degradation, phase change, and heat transfer. The proposed methodology provides a computational framework for modeling thermomechanical properties of polymers during crystallization under deformation. The limitations of this research include the narrow range of material parameters used for model validation and the absence of comparative studies with other established models. Future work will involve validating the proposed methodology against a broader range of experimental data and conducting sensitivity analyses to assess the model's performance. The developed code is available for download from a public repository. The proposed methodology offers significant advantages over existing models due to its ability to simulate stress-strain curves observed during uniaxial tension tests on polyethylene samples by modeling the rate of change of molecular weight. A thorough examination of the magnetic susceptibility in superconducting materials, specifically with a $d$-wave symmetry, reveals a positive and dispersive $\chi(\mu)$ across the Fermi surface, particularly at its topological features. This phenomenon is attributed to the interplay between the magnetic field, superconductivity, and the unique topology of the Fermi surface. In general, the magnitude of $\chi(\mu)$ is found to be substantial in comparison to other factors influencing $\chi(\mu)$, such as the superconducting gap parameter or the Fermi momentum. A dimensionless quantity, $\chi(\mu)/\chi_0$, where $\chi_0$ is the susceptibility in the absence of superconductivity, is calculated as a function of the chemical potential $\mu$ within the $d$-wave scenario. A characteristic "Fermi surface topography" emerges in $\chi(\mu)/\chi_0$, reflecting the distinct shapes of the Fermi surface's local maxima, saddle points, and van Hove singularities. The magnitude of $\chi(\mu)/\chi_0$ is found to be significantly enhanced at the outer edges of the Brillouin zone, particularly at the $(\pi, \pi)$ point, where the wave function exhibits nodal characteristics. The impact of an on-site disorder on $\chi(\mu)/\chi_0$ is also investigated, revealing a tendency towards localization that affects the topology of the Fermi surface. Recent advances in natural language processing are largely driven by the development of deep learning models, however the underlying mechanics of how these models make inferences remains poorly understood. To better grasp the functioning of neural models, the current study uses if-then statements with specific relation types such as cause and effect, whole/part relationships etc. as a simple inference framework, and observes that models can be more effectively trained when presented with this hierarchical structure. The study discovers that models are capable of identifying the relation type between statements even without explicit labeling, and that they organize relations into a hierarchical pattern similar to human conceptions, with more specific relations being subcategories of more general ones. By leveraging this property, the study shows that models can be trained to recognize the type of relation implied by a statement, and that this improves their performance on a related task known as textual common sense reasoning. The study further finds that models benefit from training on relation types even when the actual question does not mention the relation, but rather when the question and answer are presented together, indicating that models are capable of making inferences based on implicit context similar to human beings. The study's findings are confirmed across multiple models, and it is observed that models with a larger capacity tend to benefit more from the training on relation types, and that the optimal hierarchy structure can be determined automatically from statement pairs rather than relying on human input. The study's conclusions are further validated by conducting an additional experiment where models are presented with abstract relation types and it is observed that models are more likely to generate statements that are consistent with the defined relation type when compared to a control group, indicating an improvement in their inductive ability. The current study contributes to the understanding of the functioning of neural models through the lens of natural logic, and provides evidence that models can be made more effective by being trained on the hierarchical structure of if-then relation types, and that models are capable of making inferences from implicit context. The study's findings also shed light on the design of models and data generation methods, and it is hoped that the methodology employed in the current study can be utilized as a foundation for the development of more advanced models and data generation techniques that are inspired by the underlying mechanics of natural logic. The models used in the current study are pre-trained on massive text corpora consisting of over a million texts of up to 500 words in length, and it is observed that models are capable of making inferences based on relations that are implicit in the text even without explicit labeling, and that the optimal hierarchy structure can be determined automatically

The HHL algorithm determines the expectation value when applying a matrix to a random quantum state, however its practical implementation is hindered due to the squares of large numbers being divided, which is challenging for Near-term Intermediate-scale Quantum devices. To overcome this difficulty, we've developed the NISQ-HHL protocol, which approximates this expectation value using device-native operations, without the need for ratio calculations. This new approach utilizes the qubit amplitude distribution to estimate the matrix product, and our results show that it efficiently achieves accurate expectations on up to 32 qubits devices, outperforming the original HHL for complex matrices with moderate dimensions. Moreover, our method provides an adjustable trade-off between product accuracy and qubit utilization, allowing it to be suitable for a broad range of applications, and we've demonstrated its effectiveness on realistic problem scenarios with both random and real-world data. Our research paves the way for the HHL algorithm's implementation on existing and future quantum hardware. This work is relevant to a variety of domains, including chemistry, materials science, and machine learning, and our code is available online for community use.

To enhance the integration of linguistic knowledge and speech features in ASR systems, a bidirectional attention mechanism (BiAM) is introduced to our end-to-end fully neural network model. Inspired by the way humans process language, BiAM simulates a conversation between the listener (ASR) and a knowledgeable partner (linguistic knowledge) by employing a bidirectional attention mechanism. This results in a speaker-specific linguistic condition that is factored into the hidden space and used to guide the inference of posterior probabilities. Experiments indicate that our BiAM-based model yields superior word error rates (WER) compared to the standard neural network-based baseline, particularly when trained on large datasets. Our proposed method demonstrates particular efficacy when addressing out-of-domain problems, with a notable 12.3% reduction in WER when transferring to a domain with twice the distance from the reference domain compared to the baseline. Our code is available online at https://github.com/zhengzhong123/BiAM-ASR.

Consider a one-dimensional grid of size $n$, where cars arrive at random at a rate of $r$ per step, and empty spaces are prioritized for safety reasons. The goal is to determine the probability that the first $k_n$ available spaces are located within a certain range of a random starting point, as the grid size and the number of spaces in question change. As the grid size grows, we establish conditions under which the distribution of the first $k_n$ available spaces converges to a specific limit, which can be either a continuous or a discrete distribution, depending on the rate at which the grid size increases. We also establish that the convergence is asymptotically unbiased, meaning that the expected value of the corresponding limit is approximately equal to half the grid size, under certain conditions. Furthermore, we derive explicit formulas for the limit distribution, which enables us to investigate its properties, including its variance, which can be either fixed, increase with the grid size, or converge to a specific value. We frame our results in the context of two distance metrics: total variation distance and Kolmogorov distance. Systematic investigations of our problems and solutions involve formulating and solving associated continuous-time random walk problems, which yield actionable insights. We validate the accuracy of our findings through comparative analysis of our proposed methods with existing Monte Carlo simulation-based statistical inference approaches, employing Monte Carlo simulations to demonstrate the practical applicability of our research. Our discoveries are further illustrated through numerical examples and graphical representations, which provide tangible, data-driven visualizations of theoretical findings. Our research contributes to the broader context of statistical inference from random walks in continuous time, which encompasses a wide range of relevant phenomena, including random walk models with time-dependent or heterogeneous step lengths, exchangeable sequences, and certain voting systems, among others. Our work also introduces several novel research questions, such as the asymptotic behavior of the last zero of a random walk with steps drawn from an exchangeable sequence, which presents theoretical challenges that motivate future research. We develop a non-parametric maximum likelihood estimator specifically tailored for grid-based observation, which enables us to apply our findings to a voting system model, solutions to which can be interpreted as recovering the original random walk step lengths from a mixture of exchangeable sequences. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the practical applicability of our theoretical discoveries through Monte Carlo simulations, which are further discussed in the context of their limitations. Our work also offers insights into the asymptotic properties of the non-parametric maximum likelihood estimator, which can be extended to other discrete observation problems

The integration of superconducting nanowires into sensitive voltage meters requires adjustable threshold voltages. Researchers found that nanowire sensors can adapt to varying reference voltages by altering the critical voltage at which they transition to superconductivity. To understand and control this behavior, a theoretical model based on Josephson junction arrays was developed, accounting for the effects of applied DC voltages on the nanowire's electromagnetic properties. This approach enables the design of nanowire-based meters with precision-adjustable threshold voltages, effective for use in harmonic voltage measurement. Furthermore, it paves the way for developing voltage standards based on nanowire sensors, with the potential to provide a new basis for defining voltage units. Experimental validation of the model was conducted using a specific device, demonstrating the practical applicability of this approach.

Researchers have made significant progress in predicting videos from novel viewpoints using a single frame, and the success of these methods has been linked to the use of graph convolutional networks, which operate on a dual graph representation. To build on this, a novel framework is presented that includes a mechanism for automatically generating a dual representation, specifically a graph of spatial correspondence, which facilitates the prediction of videos from novel viewpoints. Unlike previous methods that rely on pre-specified graphs, the proposed framework generates a score for the optimal dual representation using a co-attention mechanism, thereby eliminating the need for manual specification. Experimentally, the proposed framework delivers superior performance when predicting videos from novel viewpoints, particularly when the target viewpoint is distant, as measured by the Viewpoint Prediction Dataset and the recently introduced VIPX dataset. The advantages of the proposed framework hold promise for similar tasks like the prediction of images from novel viewpoints. The code for the proposed framework is available online at the GitHub repository https://github.com/zwang-vslab/VIPX-Prediction. A crucial component in quantum communication systems is the phase beam splitter, which controls the reflection and transmission of photons based on their color or spatial pattern. To address scaling challenges and minimize loss of information, researchers are exploring the potential of higher-order photonic modes in design improvements. By applying the Jacobi method to a parametric family of unitary matrices, we derive an explicit expression for a phase beam splitter that operates on both spatial and frequency domains. This domain-agnostic approach enables the design of a versatile beam splitter that accurately modulates both higher-order photonic modes and their corresponding frequencies. By simulating a quantum memory implementation, our model demonstrates a significant reduction in information loss and improved scalability. The findings presented here provide a foundation for developing robust and efficient phase beam splitters capable of managing complex photonic systems effectively. The proposed framework facilitates the development of efficient and robust phase beam splitters, capable of managing both spatial and frequency-based photonic systems, and the associated code is available online. The code allows for the simulation of both lossy and lossless beam splitter implementations, and the findings are pertinent to the design of quantum memory systems. In quantum mechanics, we employ linear combinations of states to describe both particles and systems of particles. For hadrons like baryons, various combinations of quarks generate distinct sets of mass spectra in their resonance patterns. Our research utilizes the Fock-Hartree method to analyze quark systems consisting of three non-interacting components, with two of these components being considered "spectators" and the third being "active". We provide explicit equations for mass levels and probabilities in quark systems with one active quark, and explore both spinless and spinning scenarios. Furthermore, we outline a three-dimensional harmonic oscillator model to describe the internal structure of quarks, which enables us to derive precise predictions for mass splittings and level spacings in quark systems. Our approach is particularly effective in explaining the resonant mass spectra of mesons and baryons. Our results also compare favorably with experimental data from sources like the BaBar and LHCb collaborations. Our model can be further applied to predict results for other hadronic particles and systems. Our research demonstrates how quark-level physics can be utilized to interpret phenomena observed at high-energy particle accelerators. Our approach may also be used to study non-perturbative quark interactions by comparing the mass differences of isospin multiplets among hadronic particles. In recent years, research on respiratory viral transmission has given rise to various mathematical models, each attempting to capture different environmental conditions through differential equations. However, these models often require further simulation within more comprehensive framework due to their simplicity. A specific model, often referred to as the well-mixed model, has specifically been applied to predict aerosolized substance distribution, including those present in coughed-up particles, following a short time frame of $10$ seconds. When compared to more complex models, the well-mixed model tends to overestimate the peak concentration of these particles by a factor of $6.6$ or $3.1$ within the $10$ second time frame, assuming the particles are suspended in air rather than stuck to a surface or on human skin. A subsequent analysis reveals that the well-mixed model's limitations become more apparent when considering factors like gravity, airflow, and coalescence of droplets, which can result in the fusion of multiple particles equivalent to one $10$ second cough. Ultimately, the model's simplifications lead to an overestimation of aerosolized particle concentrations by a factor of $66$ or $31$ within the $10$ second time frame, depending on whether the particles are suspended in the air or not. A critical examination of these findings may influence the current guidelines aimed at mitigating the transmission of respiratory viruses. A call to action is made for conducting experimental verification of the predicted aerosolized particle distribution following a cough, which could provide a direct and precise measurement of the factors influencing virus transmission. A potential pathway for achieving this goal involves using high-speed imaging in conjunction with cough-induced particle analysis to better understand the dynamics of respiratory virus transmission. The Hall effect in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers has been studied and shows a surprising decrease in scattering with increasing Bismuth layer thickness. To understand this behavior, we used a new model that takes into account the interaction between Bismuth layers and the upper and lower interfaces of the multilayer stack. Based on this model, we found that the scattering mechanism in these multilayers is primarily influenced by the Bismuth layers, rather than the Cobalt layers. To be more precise, we observed that the mean free path of the electrons varies inversely with the number of Bismuth layers, and can be used to calculate the electron mean free path. Additionally, we used this model to modify the standard four-terminal resistance measurement methodology, and our proposed technique measures the true resistivity of the material with minimal interference from sample geometry. To verify the validity of our model, we compared the electron mean free path calculated from Hall resistance measurements with the mean free path calculated from four-terminal resistance measurements, and found that they are equal within a 10% margin of error. To further validate our model, we calculated the electron mean free path using a theoretical model based on the Cobalt layer thickness, and compared it with experimental data, and found that they are directly proportional to each other. To explore the possibility of achieving large anomalous Hall effect in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers, we calculated the spin polarization of the Bloch states in Bismuth layers using a theoretical model, and found that they increase with the number of Bismuth layers, but are limited by the formation of anti-parallel spins at the upper and lower interfaces of the multilayer stack. To overcome this challenge, we proposed a new design for the multilayer stack, in which the Bismuth layers are sandwiched between two layers of Cobalt, and calculated the expected spin polarization of the Bloch states in this new design, and found that they can achieve very high values with only a few nanometers of Bismuth layer thickness. To experimentally verify our proposed design, we suggest measuring the spin polarization of the Bloch states using photoelectron spectroscopy, and suggest possible materials that can be used as alternatives to Bismuth layers. To explore the possibility of achieving large anomalous Nernst effect in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers, we calculated the thermal diffusion length of the electrons and the heat carriers in these multilayers, and found that they are equal within a 10% margin of error. We investigate how the $p$-norm used in a neural network affects its behavior when the Lipschitz constant is constrained. Our main finding shows that with an appropriate $p$-norm, a neural network can achieve a bounded Lipschitz constant without sacrificing its classification accuracy. To demonstrate this, we develop a specific neural network that excels in both performance and Lipschitz regularity and then train it using a regression-based method. Our approach involves controlling the loss function to minimize both classification errors and the $p$-norm of the weight updates. By optimizing this combined loss, the neural network acquires both desired properties. To facilitate efficient training, we create a customized optimizer that can handle a broad range of $p$-norms, including an annealing mechanism to adapt the $p$-norm over time. Our experiments cover multiple $p$-norms, hyperparameter settings, and datasets to validate the effectiveness of our approach. Interestingly, we found that the choice of $p$-norm significantly impacts the network's ability to meet both performance and regularization criteria, and our proposed method consistently outperforms alternative approaches based on fair baselines. Moreover, our optimized neural network can generalize well to new tasks and is more resistant to adversarial attacks. To facilitate further research, we open-source our code and pre-trained models on GitHub. Our main code repository is available at https://github.com/zhongyury/LipNeuralNetwork. Our trained model repositories are available at https://github.com/zhongyury/LipNeuralNetworkModels. Our research was supported by the National Science Foundation under grant IIS-2037592. Our findings contribute to the understanding of how $p$-norms influence neural networks and provide a practical solution for training models with both high performance and low adversarial risk. Our approach can be applied to various tasks, including image classification, where our experiments show that models trained with our method are less susceptible to adversarial attacks and can classify new images more accurately. Our method is particularly effective for tasks with limited training data, and our results demonstrate the value of constraining the Lipschitz constant in such cases. Our approach is complementary to other regularization techniques and can be used in conjunction with transfer learning to achieve both performance and generalization goals. Our code and model repositories are available at https://github.com/zhongyury/LipNeuralNetwork and https://github.com/zhongyury/LipNeuralNetworkModels, respectively. We have developed a full implementation of NLO plus next-to-leading order (NLO+PS) signal simulations using the Sherpa event generator, specifically for the production of vector leptoquarks in $pp$ collisions at the LHC. By integrating the MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO interface with Sherpa's tools, we have created a vector leptoquark signal model that can generate NLO+PS predictions for signal processes, thereby significantly improving the accuracy of these simulations, particularly when reconstructing leptoquark resonances via decay products. By comparing our NLO+PS results with existing NLO signal simulations and incorporating theoretical estimates of NLO corrections, we have established a set of guidelines to ensure the consistency of NLO+PS predictions with their NLO counterparts, with variations in NLO+PS predictions at the level of 10%. Furthermore, we have explored strategies for optimizing NLO+PS signal simulations by adjusting the integration options for the virtual and real correction components, and have demonstrated the importance of valid NLO+PS signal simulations for accurately modeling signal processes, especially in scenarios with large acceptance regions around the leptoquark mass, where near-threshold production processes may need to be simulated with a higher precision of 1%. Given these findings, we recommend using NLO+PS signal simulations for vector leptoquark searches in the top-quark decay channel, and have made our generator code publicly available within the Sherpa repository. Additionally, we have outlined potential future developments, including integrating NLO+PS signal simulations with semi-leptonic and hadronic final states and developing more efficient NLO+PS matching algorithms, and have provided theoretical predictions for existing LHC search results analyzed with ATLAS and CMS. The Sherpa vector leptoquark signal model can be accessed via the following link: https://gitlab.com/phenix sherpa-vlq. A deep learning-based approach is proposed to enhance the quality of low-dose PET images by leveraging complementary information from MRI scans, without the need for paired training data.  A deep neural network framework, specifically a U-Net, was developed to simultaneously process both low-density PET and MRI scans, producing high-quality PET images at standard doses.  Utilizing Atlas-based registration, NiftyReg software was employed for precise alignment of input PET and MRI scans.  The developed model was tested on 10 individual subjects who had undergone both low-dose and standard-dose PET scans, as well as co-registered MRI scans.  The results showed significant improvements in image quality metrics, including the coefficient of variation, pointing to the potential effectiveness of this technique in clinical settings.  However, certain limitations of the study, such as limited subject sample size and absence of quantitative assessment of lesion detection, necessitate future research.  The code for this research is available on GitHub at the link https://github.com/ghoury/LD-PET-Reconstruction.  This work was supported by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada and the Alberta Cancer Foundation.  This research was presented at the International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention held in September 2020 in the paper titled "Low-Dose PET Image Reconstruction Using Deep Learning and Prior Information from MRI" [1].  Another related study can be found in the following paper: "Deep Learning Commodity Grade MRI-Gated PET Reconstruction with Prior Images" by Y. Xue, et al.  [2].  Both aforementioned studies explored similar deep learning-based methods for PET image reconstruction but utilized paired training data consisting of both low-dose and standard-dose PET scans for each subject.  In contrast to these studies, the current research utilized commodity-grade MRI scans in place of prior images derived from the same subject. The integration of contextualized embeddings into neural coreference systems has significantly improved their performance. Building on the success of the paper "Investigating Rich Sense Expressions in Neural Coreference" from 2020, this study further explores the relationship between coreference and centering theory using contextualized embeddings. Our main contribution involves conducting multiple experiments on the Alamoudi dataset, where we evaluate a state-of-the-art neural coreference system using the ACCIO framework and find that the system's performance is inconsistent with centering theory. To better align coreference with semantic meaning, we propose two contextualized neural coreference models: one with dynamically updated coreference relations based on the context, and a second one that incorporates syntactic dependencies. Our experiments show that these models perform coreference tasks more consistently with centering theory than a baseline system. To facilitate reproducibility, the code and Alamoudi dataset annotations are made publicly available. Our findings highlight the potential applications of centering theory in guiding the development of neural coreference systems. Our research also sheds light on potential limitations of current systems and suggest areas for future improvement. Our work is part of a larger project that aims to bridge the gap between semantic meaning and coreference relations using contextualized embeddings, and has implications for the development of more semantically informed coreference systems. To facilitate knowledge sharing, the Alamoudi dataset annotations are made publicly available on Zenodo, a trusted repository managed by CERN, following the guidelines set by the original dataset creators. Our code is available on GitHub, a popular platform for open-source development. Our research contributes to a broader project that explores the relationship between coreference and semantic meaning, and showcases the utility of centering theory in this context. Our work is particularly relevant to researchers and developers working on coreference systems and related tasks, such as semantic role labeling and natural language inference. Our findings also offer insights for researchers interested in the theoretical aspects of coreference and semantic meaning, and may inspire the development of new evaluation metrics that prioritize semantic consistency. Our code and dataset annotations are designed to facilitate reproducibility, and our research aims to stimulate further innovation in the field. Accurate distance estimation between WiFi access point (AP) readings, also known as fingerprints, is crucial for various location-based services. However, estimating the geospatial distance between these readings, which contain signal strength information, is not always straightforward due to the complex nature of wireless signal propagation. To address this challenge, we propose an innovative approach using a deep learning-based technique called graph convolutional neural networks (GCNN) to estimate the geospatial distance between WiFi fingerprints. This model leverages the physical location information of each reading and its associated signal strength values to produce a distance matrix. To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed technique, we conducted several experiments using two separate datasets in office and campus settings, and the results showed significant improvements in distance estimation accuracy compared to conventional machine learning models and traditional signal strength-based methods. To facilitate reproducibility, the code for this research is publicly available on GitHub. Our proposed technique demonstrates a promising solution for estimating geospatial distance between WiFi fingerprints and has practical implications for various location-based services, especially in scenarios with limited positioning information. To further improve the accuracy of distance estimation, we suggest exploring additional environmental factors, such as temperature and humidity, which can influence wireless signal propagation, and developing a hybrid technique that combines GCNN with traditional signal strength-based methods. To ensure reproducibility, we are providing the code for our research on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/ali-khodabandelvi/gcn_wifi_fingerprint_distance_estimation. To access the code, please contact the corresponding author at the following email address: a.khodabandelvi@tue.nl. To access the datasets used in this research, please contact the respective owners as follows: the first dataset can be obtained from the author of the paper 'Crowdsourcing WiFi Map Construction using Spatial Histograms' presented at the IEEE International Conference on Communications, and the second dataset can be obtained from the author of the paper 'Constructing Accurate Map of WiFi Signal Strength using Mobile Crowd Sensing' presented at the IEEE International Conference on Communications. As the number of passes increases in an energy recovery linac, the impact of beam-RF interactions becomes more significant, particularly due to the repeated exposure of sensitive radiofrequency (RF) systems to charged particles, which can lead to power loss and the formation of dark currents. To mitigate this effect, varying cavity filling patterns can be employed, which, however, influences beam dynamics and may result in the creation of dark beams above threshold, making it essential to choose an optimal filling strategy. Utilizing a single-pass model, the relationship between beam current and cavity filling was examined, revealing multiple stable states, which can be either charged or dark, depending on filling conditions. To achieve optimal performance, an appropriate filling pattern should be selected such that the first dark state occurs only when the beam current reaches its desired operating level, which is the subject of this research. An analytical approach was employed to determine the filling pattern, initially for constant beam energy, and subsequently for linear relationships between beam energy and fill pattern parameters. The aim is to ensure that the first dark state occurs at the desired current, which is either equal to zero or any other specified current, based on linear models. To validate the proposed method, Monte Carlo simulations were used. The outcome indicates that the chosen filling pattern successfully avoids the formation of dark beams above the threshold current, which can be either zero or any other specified current, within the scope of this research, which focused on linear relationships between beam energy and fill pattern parameters. The proposed approach provides a practical solution for addressing beam-RF interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs, which can be challenging to simulate numerically, and offers valuable insights into the interplay between beam current, cavity filling patterns, and radiofrequency systems. The developed method is particularly beneficial for existing energy recovery linacs experiencing power loss due to beam-RF interactions, which can be rectified simply by adjusting cavity filling patterns. The research also highlights potential difficulties in achieving threshold currents other than zero, which may require alternative approaches, and underscores the significance of careful consideration of radiofrequency system exposure limits in the design of future energy recovery linacs. The value of this study lies in its practical nature, as it addresses an important issue encountered in the course of developing LINACs for the new medical and industrial applications mentioned earlier. We investigate the free energy associated with stretching in polymer brushes situated on curved surfaces, assuming these surfaces can be accurately described using uniform, convex convolutions of a reference surface, and a Gaussian or harmonic chain polymer model. The free energy is analyzed as it relates to the mean squared end-to-end distance of the polymers, specifically for convolutions with increasing curvature, and it is observed that positive concavity holds, implying that the free energy will always increase for an expanding surface, regardless of its shape. Additionally, the relationship between the free energy and the mean squared end-to-end distance is found to be directly proportional for a given surface convolution, and this proportionality can be determined from the characteristics of the original surface. The effects of temperature and the root mean square end-to-end distance of the polymers on free energy are also examined, showing an exponential dependence on both factors. The results presented in this study provide a comprehensive understanding of the free energy associated with stretching in polymer brushes on curved surfaces. The proportionality relationships identified here can be utilized in scaling analyses of additional problems involving polymer brushes, including those on randomly expanding or changing surfaces. The value of explicitly expressing free energy in terms of mean squared end-to-end distance becomes apparent when examining the dynamics of polymer brushes using the Alexander-de Gennes model, where the mean squared end-to-end distance serves as a key dynamic variable that is directly related to the free energy. The research conducted in this study can be extended to brush geometries with varying shapes, such as spherical or cylindrical surfaces, by using the methods developed for convex convolutions. The dynamics of polymer brushes on expanding or changing surfaces will exhibit time-dependent mean squared end-to-end distance, making the introduction of an appropriate time-dependent variable, such as the root mean square end-to-end distance, essential for completing scaling analyses of these systems. The investigation into the effects of surface curvature on free energy can be generalized to include non-uniform curvature, leading to specific results for spherical and cylindrical surfaces, and demonstrating positive concavity for an expanding surface, regardless of its shape, and providing the proportionality relationships for these specific cases. The research conducted in this study aligns with the broader category of polymer brush dynamics as described by the Alexander-de Gennes model, and specifically builds upon the preceding work conducted by Di Carlo et al. Given a graph G = (V, E), the geodesic distance between two vertices i and j is the fewest number of edges in an i-j path. Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) exhibit complex behavior, making it challenging to accurately describe their variability through long-term observations. Traditional methods relying on autocorrelation and cross-correlation analyses have significant limitations due to their sensitivity to data gaps, limiting the effectiveness for data sets with incomplete observations. Additionally, these methods fail to account for the period variability components, which are crucial for interpreting the results. We present a novel approach using a mathematical model that incorporates damped harmonic components to analyze the variability of 13 AGNs based on extensive optical data sets spanning multiple decades. This method assumes that the power spectral density of the variability follows a specific pattern, which we term the 'd donut' shape, consisting of a central peak representing the harmonic component and a surrounding ring representing the remaining variability. By fitting this model, we determined the 'donut' width and depth of the harmonic component for each AGN, which we used to interpret their behavior based on their optical luminosity and the time frame of the observations. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that the harmonic component may be related to the self-intersection of light curves with long periods, which could provide valuable insights into the physics underlying the variability of these systems. We also present a comprehensive study of the challenges faced when analyzing the variability of these systems and the limitations of the data sets used, as well as the potential for future observations with increased sensitivity and duration. Our research highlights the significance of considering harmonic components in modeling the power spectral density of these systems and the necessity of extensive observations to uncover their intricate variability patterns. In the context of multi-agent decision-making, having access to agents' true valuation functions is not always feasible, prompting the study of valuation methods based on bipartite matchings and directed graphs by our research team. Initially presented in [1, 2], these techniques can approximate social welfare, verifiable payments, and other valuable quantities with various guarantees. However, the problem of approximating welfare within a factor of 1+ε of its optimal value using polynomial-time algorithms was left unresolved in previous work. Our recent investigation addresses this unexplored challenge and provides a general algorithm for achieving a (1+ε)-approximation of social welfare efficiency, building on a specific valuation method that approximates welfare within a factor of 1+2√k, where k represents the number of items in question. It's worth noting that achieving a guarantee of 1+ε approximations is possible only when agents' true values are effectively limited to values of the form 1, 1+1/ε, 1+2/ε, up to a maximum of 2+ε, for all the tested scenarios. Our research also extends the applicability of previously established results, enabling the construction of specific valuations that can yield a (1+ε)-approximation of social welfare efficiency for any number of items, in addition to providing an alternative proof of the guarantee associated with a particular form of valuations that was initially proposed in [3]. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate the potential for a broad class of algorithms that provide a constant factor approximation of social welfare efficiency, using a wide range of valuation methods based on bipartite matchings and directed graphs, without being affected by the computational complexity of the underlying problem. In contrast, the instances that we constructed in the past studies can be solved by a greedy algorithm with values of 2^k, 3^k, and (k+1)^k for the respective valuations, without any dependence on the desired level of approximation.
