Immersive video viewing experiences are hindered by the challenge of predicting user viewports.  A key factor in effective video delivery is ensuring that only necessary video data is transmitted.  To address this issue, a machine learning-based viewport prediction model is proposed, leveraging additional video information beyond just the visual content.  Specifically, the model utilizes video subtitles in addition to the video frames to improve prediction accuracy.  In testing, the proposed approach showed significant enhancements in viewport prediction accuracy, with an average improvement of 15.6% when using only the first frame as a reference, and 10.1% when comparing to a baseline model utilizing just video frames, despite increasing computational costs by 20%.  The validity of these results was further confirmed through alternative analysis, indicating potential applications in optimizing video delivery for immersive experiences, online streaming platforms, and virtual reality technology.  The code and dataset for this research are available online.  Future enhancements to the model are also discussed, including utilizing other text-based video metadata, integrating audio signals, and developing a real-time viewport prediction system, thereby paving the way for improved immersive video delivery technologies.  This work is relevant to industries utilizing video streaming services, virtual reality, and augmented reality, as well as online education platforms and video sharing websites.  In particular, companies like YouTube, Vimeo, Facebook, and Netflix may benefit from this research by optimizing their video streaming services, thereby reducing data transmission costs and enhancing user viewing experiences.  In addition to its practical implications, this study may also contribute to the advancement of machine learning technology by providing a novel approach to predicting user viewports, which in turn may foster the development of other machine learning models leveraging external audio and video information.  In evaluation tests, the proposed approach showed accuracy rates of 71.4% when predicting viewports from video frames alone, and 86.5% when using video and audio subtitles, which may serve as baseline performance measures for comparable future research models.  To facilitate replication and advancement of this research, the code and dataset utilized in this study are available online, which include 1200 videos with corresponding viewports, video frames, audio signals, and subtitles, as well as the machine learning code utilized to validate the proposed approach.  Future research directions are also discussed, which may involve developing real-time viewport prediction systems, integrating additional video metadata, and exploring machine learning models that leverage audio signals from videos. We've developed a novel method for constructing projected entangled pair states (PEPS) with a significantly reduced bond dimension, capable of approximating both thermal states and time-evolved systems in 1D quantum systems using matrix product states (MPS). Our approach, referred to as PEPS with efficient local optimizations (PEPOs), involves a direct and efficient conversion of relevant MPS characteristics, bypassing the need to employ powerful variational methods. The efficiency of our PEPO framework is demonstrated through the approximation of both a quench scenario and the thermal equilibrium state in the Heisenberg chain, where the required bond dimension scales polynomially with system size. The accuracy of our results is verified by comparing with existing methods using the bond dimension and total entropy as figures of merit. The developed PEPO framework offers a promising quantum-classical interface for efficient simulation of various quantum systems using a conventional computer. The corresponding code has been made publicly accessible as part of the TeNPy Library. The relevant data has been deposited in the NIST Archives and the code has been deposited in the GitHub Archives. The role of renormalization effects at very low energies, specifically the impact of infrared renormalons, is being considered to evaluate the gluon distribution within nucleons using jet production data. This distribution, denoted as $xG(x,Q^2)$, is essentially a measure of the probability that a parton participates in a strong interaction at a given energy $Q^2$. In this research, the gluon distribution is calculated under the assumption that the hadronic interactions are primarily driven by quarks and gluons, which are treated as random fields, and the resulting expression is expanded in a power series. The power series is then analyzed to determine the energy dependence of the gluon distribution. Since the power series is infinite, it is necessary to establish an appropriate "cutoff" based on the energy scale, which introduces an inherent uncertainty of several percent in the gluon distribution estimation, particularly at low energies. This is because the energy scale can shift the series towards either the high-power end, making it less reliable, or towards the lower-power end, making it more reliable. This effect becomes more pronounced at lower energies, resulting in an increased uncertainty of about $20\%$ in the gluon distribution at $1\ GeV^2$, as measured using jet production data from fixed-target experiments. Moreover, the development of more precise hadron colliders will make the gluon distribution more uncertain due to the energy scale at which the series becomes unstable, making it essential to address the infrared renormalization effects that contribute an increased uncertainty of about $10\%$ in the gluon distribution at $10\ TeV$, as predicted for future hadron colliders. This research also explores the relationship between the gluon distribution and other hadronic properties, such as hadron form factors and hadron masses, which are influenced by the same underlying quark and gluon fields, and as such, share similar energy dependence characteristics. This specific design allows for unique interference between a particular Rayleigh anomaly and surface plasmon resonance modes at different crystal lattice sites. Theoretical calculations using the method of multiple reflections and the transfer matrix technique revealed the existence of a magnetic field-dependent resonance shift and alteration of resonance width. The appearance of a new resonance, resulting from the interference between the surface plasmon and the Rayleigh anomaly, was also observed. This new resonance exhibited an exceptionally large optical magnetic field-induced shift of approximately 13.7 nm per kilotesla. The presence of this interference significantly enhanced the magneto-optical spectral features, revealing a very large magnetic field-induced effect in a particular resonance width and shift scenario. The influence of surface roughness on the resonance was also examined, demonstrating that even with relatively high surface roughness, the resonance remains resistant to decay. The unique properties of this magnetophotonic crystal layer make it an attractive component for magnetic field-sensitive photonic devices, with potential applications in high-sensitivity magnetic field measurement systems, particularly those utilizing the magneto-optical effect in near-infrared spectral ranges. Knowledge distillation is a significant technology for building efficient neural networks, and decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, which relies on predictions from a teacher network instead of intermediate activations, has been proven highly effective in this area. Unlike conventional knowledge distillation methods, decision-based black-box knowledge distillation does not require access to the teacher network's intermediate data, making it appealing for scenarios where only the teacher network's output is available, such as in classification tasks. This paper investigates the limitations of current decision-based black-box knowledge distillation algorithms and finds that they are primarily data-efficient models, but can be difficult to apply to continuous value prediction tasks like regression, time series forecasting, and quantity-related classification due to the scalar nature of the targets. To address this challenge, a new decision-based black-box knowledge distillation framework is proposed, targeting continuous value prediction tasks and an illustrative application, a quantity regression task known as the GaussBERD, is used to evaluate the proposed approach. Experimental results show that the proposed method can effectively transfer knowledge to a student network with a small dataset, outperforming traditional knowledge distillation in this scenario, and also compares favorably to the current data-efficient knowledge distillation algorithms, such as hard knowledge distillation and decision-based knowledge distillation. In particular, the proposed method delivers superior performance when targeting continuous value prediction tasks with classification models pre-trained on large image datasets, including an improvement of over 10\% in terms of mean absolute error when transferring from ResNet-50 to MobileNetV2 using the GaussBERD dataset. In addition, the paper provides valuable insights into the proposed method's performance under different pre-trained teacher network sizes and architectures, and offers practical guidelines for implementing the method, including selecting appropriate hyperparameters, and provides visual representations of the regression targets predicted by the student networks in the GaussBERD scenario. The proposed decision-based black-box knowledge distillation framework and the associated algorithms have been made available online for public use. The code can be accessed at this link https://github.com/ting101521/DB3KD. The paper also presents a new knowledge distillation dataset, the GaussBERD, which can be found at this link https://gaussberddataset.top/. The future direction of this research involves exploring ways to combine decision-based black-box knowledge distillation with other knowledge distillation algorithms, and investigating the applicability of the proposed method to additional continuous value prediction tasks, such as graph-related classification and ranking tasks. We introduce Co-Imitation Learning, a novel framework that enables agents to acquire proficient imitations in multiple tasks with minimal guidance. Unlike conventional imitative learning methods requiring expert demonstrations, our approach enables agents to generate high-quality imitations in one task and transfer this ability to other tasks without additional demonstrations. This is achieved by training two networks in a co-imitation learning framework, where one network acquires a skill-based representation and the other network, a controller, is responsible for producing actionable imitations. The networks are trained to minimize loss with respect to desired outcomes and the quality of their imitations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Co-Imitation Learning by conducting experiments in both simple control scenarios and complex 3D navigation tasks using the DeepMind Lab environment, and show that our approach outperforms comparable baselines in multiple tasks. Furthermore, our experiments highlight the benefits of Co-Imitation Learning in reducing required demonstrations and enabling agents to adapt to new tasks more efficiently. System implementation code can be found at: https://github.com/ghy1995116/CoImitationLearning.

To address this, our research manipulates the RL framework to leverage sentence structure information, utilizing tree-based action spaces that mirror the syntactic properties of source texts. Given the high dimensionality of action spaces, we employed a compressed representation to train a value function, and subsequently an policy model. Our experiments showed that action space optimization yields improved results when the quality of source texts increases, and our proposed method outperforms standard RL models on WMT14 English-to-German and WMT16 German-to-English translation tasks. To validate the effectiveness of tree-based action spaces, we conducted additional experiments using synthetic data and real-world pre-trained models, and our results indicated that structured action spaces can facilitate learning when source texts have complex sentence structures. Our proposed method's limitations are also discussed, and potential strategies for addressing these limitations are suggested, including integrating global constraints and incorporating more sophisticated compressed representations. Our publicly available code can be accessed at https://github.com/zhukeberry/LTR. Our research contributes to the machine translation RL field by exploring action space optimization and providing quantitative evidence for the benefits of integrating syntactic information into RL models. Quantum information flow between an open system and its surroundings can move in both directions, depending on how operations are applied to the system. To demonstrate this effect, we use a single-qubit setup with a thermal reservoir of light, and perform both forward and backward quantum information transfer on the system. The resulting interplay of unitary dynamics and decoherence allows us to extract both positional and momentum information from the system, ultimately leading to a simultaneous collapse of both degrees of freedom. This unique scenario, characterized by the interplay of unitary and non-unitary behavior, leads to a quantum scenario of bidirectional information flow that cannot be replicated with classical systems. To further illustrate the effect, we also compare it with a similar setup using a coherent reservoir. The differences between these two scenarios reveal the distinct effects of both thermal and coherent environments on the system. To quantify the effect, we calculate the time it takes for both degrees of freedom to become completely mixed, and show how this time varies with the system's initial state and the frequency of the environment. To clarify the role of unitary dynamics in this setup, we also demonstrate how to counteract the effects of the environment on the system using counterdiabatic driving. This approach allows us to generate both degrees of freedom simultaneously, effectively erasing the effect of the environment on the system. To achieve this, we modify our system to include an additional degree of freedom that serves as a catalyst for counteracting the environment, resulting in both degrees of freedom becoming equally populated and remaining so over time. To distinguish this scenario from the initial setup, we refer to it as the 'counteradiabatic scenario'. This study delves into the underlying concurrency control mechanisms of widely used NoSQL databases, specifically MongoDB, to analyze the snapshot isolation properties in various deployments. The research focuses on three specific implementations within MongoDB: WiredTiger, Replicaset, and ShardedCluster, and determines the level of snapshot isolation for each, labeling them as Weak Isolation, Strong Isolation, or Strict Isolation. The findings reveal that WiredTiger ensures Strong Isolation, Replicaset achieves Weak Isolation, and ShardedCluster guarantees Strict Isolation. The work also identifies and evaluates possible attacks against these deployments to demonstrate the practical implications of their respective isolation levels. The research demonstrates that Replicaset and ShardedCluster are vulnerable to deadlocks and lost updates, among other issues, while WiredTiger proves resistant to these attacks. The study contributes to our understanding of the relationship between concurrency control mechanisms and snapshot isolation properties within NoSQL databases. The results highlight the significance of carefully selecting database deployment settings to balance performance, availability, and data consistency. The study further emphasizes the necessity of rigorous testing for concurrent workloads to ensure database deployments meet the requirements of specific applications. The research also offers a framework for evaluating the snapshot isolation properties of other NoSQL databases with multi-client settings. The study's findings are publicly available and can be used by the community to build upon the research. We investigated a one-dimensional Ising model with periodic boundary conditions, consisting of coupled triangles instead of the traditional nearest-neighbor interactions. This system can be reimagined as a chain of coupled spins in a triangular lattice, where each spin interacts with its two neighbors in the chain. We simulated the magnetization process of this system using Monte Carlo methods and obtained the hysteresis loop for various temperature values. Our findings showed that the hysteresis loop exhibits a symmetrical, sinusoidal shape, with the magnetization levels at the peak and trough of the loop being 1 and 0, respectively. Moreover, the loop's width decreases with increasing temperature, eventually disappearing at the critical temperature, where the system transitions from a disordered state to an ordered state. Furthermore, by analyzing the spin configuration, we identified three temperature regions: a high-temperature region where the spins are randomly arranged, a low-temperature region where the spins are aligned with an anti-ferromagnetic long-range order, and an intermediate temperature region characterized by coexisting anti-ferromagnetic and ferromagnetic ordering. In the intermediate region, the hysteresis loop's width remains nearly constant, whereas in the high-temperature region, the width scales with the square root of the applied field strength. Notably, the coexistence of anti-ferromagnetic and ferromagnetic ordering in the intermediate temperature region results from the coupling of the spins in the triangular lattice, giving rise to a field-driven phase transition within this temperature range. Our study demonstrated that the interactions between spins in a triangular lattice lead to a distinctive hysteresis loop shape and a field-driven phase transition, with the loop's width scaling in a particular manner with temperature and field strength. Our research provides a comprehensive understanding of the one-dimensional Ising model with coupled triangles and highlights the unique features of hysteresis loops in systems with competing ordering phenomena. Recent studies have revealed a stronger solar influence on the energetic requirements for spacecraft to escape from close to the Sun, specifically within 1 astronomical unit (AU), than previously expected, although the additional energy needed is currently unclear. As a result, NASA and other space agencies are reevaluating their mission designs and launch sites to better understand and account for this phenomenon. Our research proposes a new statistical model to describe how the energy required to reach escape velocity varies with heliocentric distance, incorporating both general gravitational principles and the effects of solar plasma, extreme ultraviolet radiation, and magnetic fields on a global scale. By using existing data effectively and incorporating new statistical tools, our approach provides a more accurate and universally applicable framework for estimating the energy necessary for spacecraft to escape the solar gravitational influence, particularly at close ranges. Our study utilizes recent spacecraft data, including the STEREM-1 mission, to demonstrate the applicability and benefits of this new model. Specifically, we show that the energy distributions are skewed and asymmetric, reflecting the impact of solar activity and the effects of close approaches to the Sun, and highlight the significance of accurately accounting for these factors in mission planning, particularly for missions intended to operate in the inner solar system for extended periods. Our proposed statistical model offers valuable insights to inform future space mission design, as well as provides a framework for analyzing existing data and understanding the complex solar influence on the energetic requirements for spacecraft escape velocity. Our research indicates that future space missions requiring access to close solar distances should be designed with the energy needs of escape velocities in mind, and that agencies should consider reevaluating existing mission parameters based on our findings, which demonstrate a 10 to 20 percent increase in the energy required for escape velocity within 0.5 AU, and an even more significant effect when considering the outer Earth's orbit. Our study further shows that the energy distributions are asymmetrical, with longer tails on the lower energy side, reflecting the impact of close approaches to the Sun, and that the energy required for escape velocity decreases with increasing heliocentric distance, but with a non-linear relationship. Cross-lingual emotion recognition refers to the task of utilizing a model trained in one language to recognize emotions in another language. This challenge is particularly significant when using multilingual data, as it necessitates a model that can distinguish between diverse languages while identifying emotions. To overcome this difficulty, a common approach involves training a model on mixed-language data without disentangling the languages, but this approach can suffer from style interference, hindering the model's ability to adapt to new languages and emotion categories. In response to these limitations, a proposed multi-task convolutional neural network model filters out languages from the mixed-data, enabling the model to focus on universal emotional characteristics while maintaining maximum linguistic diversity. Experimental results indicate that this approach yields significant improvements in adapting the model to new languages and emotion categories, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods according to multi-task learning metrics. Moreover, the proposed model excels in single-task emotion recognition tasks when applying it to various languages, surpassing the performance of language-specific models trained on individual datasets according to multiple evaluation metrics. Systematic analyses of model performance have been conducted through both free and constrained scenario experiments, revealing the following findings: the model performs better when there is little difference between the primary language and the target language to be recognized, the model performs worst when the primary and target languages are opposite each other in the low-resource language ranking, and the model performance improves significantly when the size of the mixed-data increases tenfold. Systematic parameter analysis further reveals that increasing the size of the mixed-data significantly improves model performance, while the impact of parameter settings on model performance is relatively minor. Experimental results have been verified through free and constrained scenario experiments on both multilingual and single-language emotion recognition datasets, comprising the following datasets: MOODS-1k, MOODS-5k, VEMOTION, VEMOTION EXTENDED, and VEMOTION EXTENDED SINGLE. Systematic code and model reproducibility have been ensured through publicly available code and model repositories. Overall, the proposed model provides significant performance improvements in cross-lingual emotion recognition tasks, demonstrating robust adaptability when recognizing emotions in diverse languages and datasets. Experimental results further reveal the model's resilience when there is little difference between the primary and target languages, as well as its ability to recognize emotions in single-language settings. Re-examining the behavior of planar shocks with extremely high pressures from a vacuum, researchers studied the effects of a strong, ideal gas-based shock in multiple dimensions using the self-similar approach. They compared their one-dimensional results to existing analyses and discovered a critical pressure ratio, beyond which shocks with extremely high pressures from a vacuum behave differently and create infinitely thick profiles. This phenomenon is accompanied by unusual profile asymmetry and the slow release of energy around the origin. Specifically, in one dimension, the dimensionless total energy released during such shocks remains constant at 2.435 times the constant pressure, and it decreases with increasing pressure ratio according to a specific power with adjustments for dimensionality. Additionally, the constant energy provides a universal explanation for the observed asymmetry. In one dimension, the shock thickness also remains constant at 1.715 times the root of the adiabatic index, and it too decreases with increasing pressure ratio. The effects of changing the adiabatic index and dimensionality on shocks with extremely high pressures from a vacuum were also compared and contrasted. The approach can be applied to other self-similar shock scenarios. The research was published in the journal Physical Review Fluids on 24 July 2024. The authors, S. S. Samsonov, A. A. A generation's socioeconomic status is substantially influenced by the opportunities allocated to its preceding generation, whose effects can persist for up to five generations, according to our analysis.  In contrast, the impact of the current generation's opportunities on their own future is minimal, i.e., less than one year, based on our mathematical formulation using a first-quadrant cone that models intergenerational relationships.  By applying this understanding to economic systems, we find that mobility within a society is largely driven by the allocation of resources and opportunities among its members rather than by chance events or group identity.  As a result, we contend that opportunity allocation resembles a public good with positive externalities that benefit future generations, whose interests are not well represented in individual decisions.  Consequently, government intervention is necessary to address societal mobility and related pressing issues like income inequality, given the inherent limitations of self-interested behavior in opportunity allocation.  Ultimately, our analysis invites a fresh perspective on the concept of opportunity cost, one that considers not only the immediate effects on an individual but also the long-term generational consequences.  In the context of economic systems, we discover that opportunity costs vary significantly across different allocations of resources and future generations, demonstrating that they are inherently multi-period multi-agent phenomena that span multiple generations of players with distinct interests, rather than one-time events affecting individual agents.  Given the far-reaching implications for future generations, we propose a new theoretical framework – based on the use of a cone that models the relationships among generations – that provides a promising starting point for ongoing research aimed at better understanding the complex interplay of opportunity costs and socioeconomic mobility within societies.  Ultimately, our analysis suggests that opportunity costs should be viewed as valuable assets that can be managed to benefit society as a whole, rather than simply being seen as expenses to be minimized for individual self-interest.  As such, our research offers a unique perspective that positions opportunity costs at the forefront of societal mobility policy discussions, given the inherent externalities that benefit future generations and the associated need for coordinated governance to effectively address them.  In the context of economic theory, our mathematical formulation using a cone that models intergenerational relationships provides a novel contribution that extends existing knowledge by incorporating multiple generations of players with distinct interests in a unified framework, thereby offering a fresh understanding of opportunity costs as valuable assets with positive externalities that benefit future generations rather than simply being viewed as costs to be minimized for individual self-interest.  As such, our research invites a paradigm shift in the way opportunity costs are perceived and managed within economic systems.

In particle accelerators, the interaction between opposing beams causes them to shift from their intended paths, and by measuring these shifts precisely, researchers can also directly determine the charged particle beam's electric field properties. To determine how charged a particle is, physicists use a dimensionless value called the anomalous magnetic moment, which can be measured with high accuracy, and by comparing this to the beam's electric property, they can determine its charged dimensionless value, known as the anomalous electric moment. By dimensionally converting this value, physicists can calculate the beam's electric property, which until now has been theoretically estimated rather than being directly measured. To determine this property, researchers need very small beam interactions, making it challenging to measure at conventional particle colliders but feasible at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). By using multiple sensitive measurements, physicists were able to quantify the beam's electric property with a high degree of precision, achieving an accuracy of one kilometer rather than the previously estimated range of ten to hundred kilometers. This achievement demonstrates that the dimensionally charged nature of high-energy particles can be measured directly and provides a promising approach for future particle beam research. We develop a generalized framework for distributed parameter estimation, within which we derive a novel algorithm that leverages neighbor-to-neighbor communication. This algorithm enables a group of non-cooperative agents to exchange information and optimize a collective objective, undeterred by the presence of malicious agents seeking to disrupt this process. Our contribution involves designing a distributed update law that effectively mitigates the impact of compromised data, thereby promoting cohesive coordination among the non-malicious agents. In turn, this facilitates a collective decision that approximates the true parameter with diminishing error, as time progresses. Moreover, we establish conditions under which the collective decision converges to its desired limit, both in the presence and absence of malicious behavior. This streamlined approach enables a broad range of applications, including distributed optimization and consensus-based protocols. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by applying it to a representative distributed estimation problem. Furthermore, our results provide key insights into the influence of various system parameters on performance, offering a pathway for optimizing these parameters to ensure seamless adaptation to dynamic environments. We investigate the capabilities of BART in a linearization task that mirrors word ordering, testing its ability to produce the most semantically accurate linear order given a set of unrelated words. In evaluating BART's performance on this task, our analysis reveals it significantly lags behind a straightforward tree linearization approach using a standard graph-based algorithm. To further examine the limitations of BART in this context, we explore two variations of the task: one where the input words have a defined linear order and another where the input consists of a set of unrelated words with varying levels of structural distance from a linear order. In both cases, our data shows that performance improves as the input words' linear order becomes more structurally similar to a random permutation. Our findings also demonstrate a significant correlation between the distance of a linear order from randomness and the associated computational cost. In contrast, the cost of our baseline algorithm remains consistently stable across different input conditions. Our research implies that over-reliance on sequence structures may hinder the generative capabilities of certain neural networks, leading to poor performance in tasks that require linearization, especially in cases with complex input relationships. Deepfake detection networks have achieved superior performance due to their ability to effectively leverage visual cues, however, these models suffer from a significant limitation - they perform poorly on unseen domains. This challenge becomes even more pronounced as the number of domains increases, making domain adaptation a necessity. In response to this need, we present a novel multi-domain deepfake detection framework that employs cross-stitch connections to connect domain-specific networks, thereby creating a unified network capable of detecting deepfakes across multiple domains. In contrast to conventional domain adaptation techniques that focus on finding a shared representation, our approach directly combines domain-specific features through learned connections. As a result, our framework exhibits improved robustness and can be scaled to an unlimited number of domains with minimal computational overhead. We validate the effectiveness of our proposed approach by conducting comprehensive experiments on the FFSDC and DeeDet datasets, covering various single-domain and multi-domain scenarios, and demonstrate significant performance enhancements over existing state-of-the-art methods. In particular, our framework achieves notable gains in the following scenarios: 1) when switching from a low-quality to a high-quality image dataset (e.g., CMU-SDC to FFMC), where our approach shows a 13.1% improvement over the current top-performing method; 2) when detecting deepfakes in multiple high-quality image datasets (e.g., FFMC, FD-Coln, and FD-SyN), where our approach shows a 21.1% improvement over the current top-performing method. Our code and models are available for public use at https://github.com/zwang84/MultiDomainDeepfakeDetection.

Our analysis indicates that a staggering 72% of Forsage users suffer financial setbacks, with the majority losing $1000 or more. To understand the scope of these losses, we examined user transaction data spanning nearly two years and aggregated $92 million in transactions involving 87,000 users worldwide. By categorizing user participation patterns, our study reveals a predictable, mathematically-based loss distribution among Forsage participants, influenced primarily by the project's guaranteed returns rather than external factors. To demonstrate the validity of our loss distribution model, we conducted multiple tests using various data subsets and found it accurately reflected past losses, with a high degree of certainty. To illustrate the practical applications of this model, we calculated the expected losses for a specific Forsage project, known as "Epic One", which totaled $52 million, based on actual data, and forecasted future losses of $13 million within the next year if the project continues at its current pace. Notably, our research reveals that the guaranteed return rates specified in pyramid schemes like Forsage are directly proportional to the projected losses, with a correlation coefficient of 0.8. Our study also highlights the difficulties in distinguishing some pyramid schemes from legitimate multi-level marketing models, citing Forsage as a prime example, and emphasizes the importance of closely examining financial guarantees and return-on-investment ratios to prevent significant financial losses among participants. To facilitate further study, our loss distribution model is applicable to a broad range of pyramid schemes, including those with guaranteed return rates below 100% and large networks of participants. To ensure transparency and reproducibility, our research is based on publicly accessible data and features executable code online. Our findings have the potential to guide regulatory agencies in identifying suspicious pyramid schemes and predicting potential financial losses among participants. To demonstrate the practical utility of our model, we conducted a simulated trial based on the allegations made against Robert Perkins and Forsage, and found that the expected losses for "Epic One" users, calculated using our model, align with the outcomes of actual Forsage user transactions. To foster a deeper understanding of the challenges faced by participants in pyramid schemes, our study emphasizes the importance of recognizing these projects as "confidence tricks" that exploit human trust and perseverance, rather than relying on complex statistical models that attribute losses to random chance. Our approach also acknowledges the critical role of guaranteed return rates in scheme designers, who deliberately manipulate financial parameters to maximize profits, and encourages regulators to examine return-on-investment ratios as key indicators of suspicious pyramid schemes. Recent surveys have uncovered numerous globular cluster candidates around the Milky Way. We investigated two likely globular clusters, J084107.55-771940.4 and J123457.90-695137.0, using archival telescopic data and a 3D stellar dynamical model of the Milky Way. Estimated ages for these clusters range between 10 to 20 billion years, placing them among the oldest cluster candidates in the Milky Way. J084107.55-771940.4 with a distance of approximately 20 kiloparsecs, exhibits a distinct double main sequence and may be affected by binary star interactions or tidal disruption. J123457.90-695137.0 at a distance of around 30 kiloparsecs, shows distinct colour and magnitude differences between its inner and outer regions, likely resulting from interactions with the Milky Way's bulge. Both clusters provide valuable insights into the evolution of the Milky Way and its surrounding environment. Additionally, an analysis of previously identified cluster, J043137.66-704435.6, with a distance of approximately 20 kiloparsecs, was also conducted. This cluster with a distance of around 20 kiloparsecs, exhibits a main sequence turnoff and may have a mass of approximately 10 to the power of 4 solar masses, based on its colour and luminosity. It is, however, unclear whether this cluster constitutes a distinct entity or is instead a component of the known globular cluster, NGC 2571. Nonetheless, further observation is required to confirm its status. This research was conducted as part of a broader study of field populations in the Milky Way's bulge using infrared telescopic data from ESO's VLT. Two clusters were successfully distinguished from field populations based on their colour-magnitude diagrams, while three others required further observation to confirm their status. This study highlights the significance of close examination of suspected globular clusters, given the limitations of initial discovery surveys, and underscores the value of multi-wavelength data in understanding the evolution of the Milky Way. Systematic investigations of cluster candidates are crucial for developing a comprehensive understanding of the Milky Way's population, particularly in its bulge region. This knowledge can be used to assess theoretical models of galaxy evolution and provides valuable context for the numerous globular clusters awaiting discovery in the Milky Way. This research leverages existing infrared telescopic data from VLT and will guide future surveys, such as the Milky Way Satellite Survey, for finding additional cluster candidates in the Milky Way's bulge. We introduce a novel class of erasure correction codes based on tensor networks, consisting of a single species of highly entangled, rank-r tensors in d dimensions, with a construction that guarantees (d-r)\*r usable information channels. These codes can accurately recover original data from at most r*(d+1) erased channels, achieving a compression ratio of approximately (d-1)/d when the input is uniformly random, as validated through simulations with up to 16 spatial dimensions. The structure of these codes allows for efficient implementation of decoding algorithms, using a combination of classical and quantum operations, and may have applications in both classical and quantum information theory. Additionally, we demonstrate that these codes can be used to correct erasures in both classical and quantum information, as well as serve as a precursor for quantum fault-tolerant logic. The specific case of rank-2 tensors in a 3D space provides a specific example of a code that can accurately recover up to 2 erased channels from a set of 3 channels. The generality of this code type allows for potential extension to quantum fault-tolerant logic in systems with arbitrary dimensional space. The corresponding code threshold, below which the code's ability to recover data degrades, can be tuned by adjusting the level of entanglement in the tensor network. Theoretical calculations and comparative analysis against existing codes hint at the potential for a class of codes with thresholds arbitrarily close to 1, with the specific case of rank-2 tensors in a 3D space having a threshold of approximately 0.73. The code construction process itself is robust and versatile, allowing for variations of the code, such as those with additional redundancy channels, and may have implications for the design of classical codes based on quantum principles. The specific case of a code with a rank of 2 in a 4-dimensional space is particularly noteworthy, as it represents a code with the lowest known rank and dimension that can correct the erasure of 2 channels from a set of 4 channels, with a threshold of approximately 0.68, and can be considered a fundamental limit for codes of this type, given its placement in the established trade-off curve in the regime of low code density. The corresponding code thesis also includes a comprehensive review of the underlying theory and relevant research in the field of quantum information science. Researchers analyzed three solar flares using high-resolution spectroscopy to precisely observe changes in certain hydrogen lines and the overall optical and far-ultraviolet energy output. Combining data from Solar Optical Spectrograph and the Solar Ultraviolet Spectral Radiation Telescope enabled a comprehensive understanding of these flares, particularly in the $1215.67$ \AA\ line of highly ionized hydrogen, which has never been directly observed on solar flares. By comparing this line to other optical and UV features, the scientists discovered a consistent relationship with other hydrogen emissions, suggesting a single source for these particles, which must be extremely hot, possibly similar in temperature to some stellar flares. Additionally, analyzing this source's duration and comparing it to other energy outputs revealed that this source exhibits a longer lifetime than other energy outputs on the sun, which could be indicative of a persistent, post-peak phase of solar flares. Lastly, modeling this line also revealed a broadening effect that might be more pronounced than previously observed in other solar flares, which could be related to the particle energy distributions during these events. Overall, the analysis of these three solar flares provides a detailed understanding of the physics governing certain hydrogen emissions and offers valuable insights into the energy output during solar flares. Similarly, these findings may also be applicable to stellar flares, given the known similarities between these two phenomena. 

Additionally, the analysis of this particular $1215.67$ \AA\ line may serve as a valuable indicator for detecting and studying flares on low-mass stars using spectrographic data from upcoming missions like PLATO and TESS, which are expected to generate extensive datasets of stellar variability and flares. By focusing on this particular line, researchers can directly measure line broadening, which, as found in this study, exhibits a consistent relationship with other optical and UV features, allowing for a comprehensive understanding of the flare physics. Given the known differences in energy output during solar flares and the potential for scaling, studying this particular line on low-mass stars through time-domain spectroscopy may reveal distinct differences in physics governing solar and stellar flares. 

Ultimately, continuous high-resolution spectroscopy of the Sun and stars can reveal a wide range of variability, from the lack of broadening in some cases to the increased duration of post-peak phases, which may hold significant implications for our understanding of the physics governing these events, particularly the energy distribution of particles during flares, and could potentially be studied through time-domain spectroscopy of stars similar to the Sun using upcoming missions.

This work explores the application of the Koopman operator theory to analyze nonlinear systems with multiple attractors in their state space. By utilizing the Koopman operator framework, our approach reconstructs the original dynamical system from a observed, simplified version of the dynamics, specifically a binary map that indicates the probability of transitioning between each state. This method allows us to extract meaningful information about the system's dynamics, including the distance between attractors, as well as the characteristics of these attractors in systems with multiple attractors. Our analysis reveals that the probability distribution associated with the binary map can be accurately modeled using a non-parametric kernel-based approach. To validate our method, we apply it to two nonlinear systems: a mechanical system with multiple attractors where we measure the displacement of a pendulum, and a biological system where we simulate the dynamics of a gene expression response to external stimuli. In both cases, our analysis successfully recovers the original dynamics from a reduced representation, demonstrating the effectiveness of the Koopman operator theory in uncovering attractor properties in complex nonlinear systems. Experimental evidence from a mechanical system shows that the method can be robust even when measurements are noisy, demonstrating the potential of this approach for practical applications. Neural text generation models like sequence-to-sequence networks with attention have been effectively used in recent times for complex text generation tasks. However, selecting optimal sentence representations to use as input can be challenging due to the dense encoding produced by these models. To address this challenge, a novel method called SparseGAN has been developed and implemented, leveraging the theory that generated texts should resemble natural statistics, specifically, by using a linear regression-based approach to decode representations into the actual text. The model's ability to generate dense representations allows for the identification of unimportant features through sparse regression, which in turn aids in eliminating superfluous sentence inputs. The results from our experiments indicate that this method leads to improved sentence representations, resulting in higher quality text generation when restricted to only the most crucial inputs. The proposed model has been successfully applied to both unconditional and conditional text generation tasks, outperforming the current state-of-the-art methods according to the metrics used, including BLEU and perplexity scores. The code for SparseGAN is available online at the GitHub repository. The developer encourages feedback and future collaboration with the community. The developer's expectation is that the method will continue to evolve through community input, leading to enhanced text generation capabilities. The search for life beyond Earth through panspermia suggests examining deceased or dying stars' residual disks for microbial habitats. Interstellar objects like comet C/2019, known as Boris, and other possible comets could provide access to these environments. We analyzed 41 spectroscopic observations of comet C/2019 and detected magnesium vapour emanating from its coma on three occasions, utilizing the VLT by the IGRINS instrument with a resolution of 7,500. Comet C/2019's magnesium spectrum showed a notable discrepancy from typical comet spectra, suggesting it originated from interstellar sources rather than solar winds. This finding could be linked to panspermia, presenting the first potential detection of microbial life associated with an interstellar comet, and highlights the need for further panspermia-based astrobiological research. We propose utilizing the VLT to generate high-resolution spectra of comet C/2019 under different conditions, aiming to confirm magnesium emissions and explore other possible elements, with the potential to shed light on possible microbial habitats in the solar system through the study of deceased stars' residual disks. Additionally, we suggest the VLT could be used to examine other comets and meteorites for signs of interstellar organic compounds, and the James Webb Space Telescope could be utilized to analyze comet C/2019's magnesium composition with higher precision, offering further insights into this discovery. The study of deceased stars' residual disks may reveal new targets for evaluating the possibility of interstellar panspermia, and the community should be prepared to investigate any future interstellar comet sightings with a biological focus. The data analysis is available online, and the IGRINS spectrum of magnesium vapour from comet C/2019 is presented. The research was conducted by the author as part of their PhD thesis at the Australian National University. The work was supported by the Australian Research Council and the Australian Federal Government, with access to the VLT provided by the European Southern Observatory. The VLT observations were managed by the European Southern Observatory, and the IGRINS data was processed using the IGRINS reduction package. The study of the magnesium spectrum relied on the MAGIOS model, and the analysis of the comet C/2019 data followed the standard procedure for cometary spectroscopy. The findings suggest that the detected magnesium emissions could result from cometary activity, solar winds, or atmospheric abductions, but given the duration and magnitude of the observations, it is more likely that the magnesium originated from an interstellar source. Accurate population density measurements are crucial for comprehending an animal's key characteristics, such as home range size and population size. However, traditional methods to estimate these characteristics are often expensive, time-consuming, or require the use of multiple technologies. Animal movement scientists have found that models based on capture-recapture in space (SCR) can provide reliable estimates of an animal's home range size and density without the need for multiple technologies. These models use data from movement tracking via GPS and a small number of initial captures. Nonetheless, SCR models typically require a substantial amount of data, which can be difficult to obtain, especially in situations where only a limited number of animals can be captured. In our study, we used a synthetic method to test a simplified SCR model under various conditions and found that this model can accurately estimate an animal's home range size and density, even with a small number of captures, primarily because it takes account of movement patterns. Our research provides a promising foundation for further development of low-cost methods to study free-ranging animals. These methods could incorporate initial captures and movement tracking via GPS, potentially leading to a universally applicable technique for animal research. 

In this study, we present a discrete-time SCR model that can estimate an animal's home range size and density based on limited captures and movement data, specifically a Markovian model that utilizes change-of-variable formulas to link movement data with traditional SCR models. Our approach assumes that an animal's probability of being detected within a specific area during a particular time period is directly related to its recent movement history. We then derive an approximate maximum likelihood estimator for the model parameters by first reparameterizing the model in terms of the home range density and size, and then utilizing the Gamma distribution to approximate the resulting non-linear system of equations. We evaluated the performance of our model using simulated movement data and found that it can accurately estimate an animal's home range size and density even with limited data, primarily due to its ability to effectively utilize movement data. Our research demonstrates the potential benefits of SCR models that incorporate movement patterns and suggests that such models could provide a versatile framework for animal research, offering multiple applications and data inputs. Systematically varying movement pattern parameters, we also investigated the effects of different movement patterns on home range size and density estimates. Our findings indicate that models based on SCR can capture the relationship between movement patterns and home range size and density, offering a unified explanation for previous research findings. Ultimately, our study reveals the advantages of using movement data from GPS tracking in conjunction with limited captures, presenting a promising data collection methodology

Networks with multiple interconnected layers are widespread and play a key role in spreading information, influencing behavior, and preventing the spread of diseases, among other phenomena. Researchers often study these networks one layer at a time due to the complexity of multilayer dynamics. Yet, this simplified approach can lead to network stability misinterpretation, particularly when interactions between different layers significantly affect node connections within individual networks. To address this challenge, the study presents a simplified approach to examining network state stability, specifically for networks composed of multiple interconnected layers without regard to time, using the concept of joint network centrality. This metric measures the influence a node has on its surrounding network, taking into account connections across different layers, and can be used to analyze network state stability, in addition to network fragmentation and community structure. By applying this approach to multilayer versions of two well-known network models, Barabasi-Albert and Erdos-Renyi networks, the study demonstrates its effectiveness and provides valuable insights into network state stability, fragmentation, and community structure, particularly with respect to single-layer network analogues. Furthermore, the research reveals the presence of a unique stability parameter that significantly impacts networks composed of multiple layers, with effects visible in both random and assortative fragmentation scenarios. The study's findings may serve as a foundation for exploring multilayer network dynamics, particularly in relation to state stability in complex systems, influenced by interactions across different layers. The proposed approach's limitations and potential enhancements for dynamic multilayer networks are also discussed. Systematic analysis of dynamic processes on multilayer networks, with multiple co-evolving layers, is also presented in the following paper: arXiv:2107.01332v2. The associated dataset is available in the following repository: https://github.com/ahmadiol/MLSNStabilityAnalysis. The code for the simulations conducted in the study is accessible in the following repository: https://github.com/ahmadiol/MLSNStabilityAnalysis/tree/main/Simulations. The study's findings have been published in the following papers: arXiv:2006.05313, arXiv:2010.05048, arXiv:2010.05049, arXiv:2012.11022, arXiv:2107.01332. Building upon the concept of differential modules introduced by Cartier and Kolster, our research expands on their theory by developing a framework for modules with differential operators in the context of Devlin-style model theory. Specifically, we demonstrate that for any computable theory T, there exists a model of arithmetic within which the differential operator $\frac{\partial}{\partial x}$ can be defined as an operator that is "parameterized" by the operator $\frac{\partial}{\partial x}$, as well as showing that this model satisfies Leibniz's rule for differential operators. Furthermore, we show that for any first-order formula $\phi(x)$, the validity of $\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(\phi(x)) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}$ within this model is equivalent to the instance where $\phi(x)$ is a differential formula. Additionally, we establish the relationship between our differential operator and the operator defined by Aczel and Hintikka within the model of arithmetic. Lastly, we establish that within this model of arithmetic, any computable function can be demonstrated to be a differential formula. Our research expands upon the theory of differential modules by providing a context for modules with differential operators defined on any computable theory, as well as offering an interpretation of the theory of arithmetic with differential operators. Ultimately, our findings contribute to the broader narrative of attempting to formalize mathematical concepts within the framework of model theory. Our research relies on the model theory of arithmetic as well as the theory of modules with differential operators, and our discoveries are motivated by the work of Aczel and Hintikka, among others. To evaluate the effectiveness of an automated testing system, developers must first overcome a significant barrier: navigating the system to identify and fix the underlying code issues. To streamline this process, we've developed an innovative algorithm that guides users through the structure of a program, pinpointing precise locations where errors are likely to occur based on historical crash data. Utilizing a mix of static program analysis and machine learning, our "Error Prediction Map" generator filters out irrelevant information, prioritizes crucial details, and highlights probable error sources, thus simplifying the testing process. Our research involves creating an automated testing environment, developing an algorithm to predict error locations, and conducting experiments to validate the efficacy of our approach. Specifically, we predict the likelihood of a program crashing in response to specific input inputs, and our results show that this approach can efficiently pinpoint 70% of the errors in a tested program with just 10% of the total possible locations to examine. Moreover, our algorithm is versatile and can be applied to various testing scenarios, including both new and existing programs. Our testing code is available online for public use.

The root system of type A7 contains the root system of type D5 as a sub-system whose maximal root is located at a distance of 2 from every root within the sub-system, albeit not all at the same angle. Conversely, the root system of type D5, with roots $\epsilon_i^2 = 0$ and $\epsilon_i \epsilon_j = -1$ for $1\le i\ne j\le 5$, can be realized using a specific Lie algebra, specifically the centralizer of a subgroup of G2 within A7. Similar properties also exist for the root system of type D4 within A6. Specifically, the maximal root of type D4, situated at the origin in a 3-dimensional space with Cartesian coordinates, lies at a distance of 2 from every root of the sub-system, at an angle of 60 degrees for the 4 non-isotropic roots. This can be realized within the Lie algebra A8, specifically within the centralizer of a subgroup of E7. This achievement allows us to explore new aspects of the 16-Generator Mathieu group M24, drawing from the characteristics of the Lie algebra E7, with both A8 and D4 sub-systems as essential components. This, in turn, leads to the discovery of a 5-parameter family of solvable groups, each with 197,409,600 generators, and the determination that the primitive action of M24 on the set of 5-subspaces in an 8-dimensional vector space over the finite field with two elements relies on just 16 generators. Furthermore, we establish an isomorphism between the automorphism group of the binary Golay code and the group of symplectic transformations of a 6-dimensional vector space over the finite field with two elements, both realized as the centralizer of a subgroup of A8. This discovery enables us to characterize the automorphism group of the extended binary Golay code, determining its structure as a group of order 403,536, consisting of 3,023,040 generators, rather than the previously reported 2,304. This achievement also leads to an exploration of the Lie algebra E7, with the resulting understanding that its centralizer within the Lie algebra E8 is equivalent to the Lie algebra of the group E7, a realization that allows for a more precise definition of the Lie algebra E7. This, in turn, facilitates the establishment of an isomorphism between the group E7 and a specific subgroup of the group E8

We propose a randomized distributed algorithm aimed at estimating the size of a specific node in a social network that follows a general random graph structure, where connections are bidirectional and weighted. This algorithm is distinctive in that it only requires access to an arbitrary neighbor, rather than a specifically chosen neighbor as in previous methods. We prove that our algorithm yields an approximate node size estimate, with the degree of approximation being directly related to the number of samples taken. Additionally, our algorithm exhibits an interesting property where the sample size it uses is independent of the network size, making it appealing for large-scale networks. We validate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm through numerical simulations using various network configurations. These simulations demonstrate that our algorithm delivers accurate size estimations across a broad spectrum of network sizes and complexities. Furthermore, our results highlight the cost-efficient nature of our algorithm, especially when compared to traditional centralized methods, where the sample size is directly proportional to the network size. Our proposed algorithm has practical implications for various real-world applications, including contact tracing in mobile networks, estimating node degrees in cognitive radio networks, and identifying influential spreaders in complex networks. Our code is available online for public access.

Accurate queue length estimation is crucial for safe and efficient traffic management, especially with the increasing popularity of cooperative adaptive cruise control systems that rely on real-time queue information. Given the limited accessibility of precise traffic data, researchers have explored various methods for estimating queue lengths using camera images and vehicle interdistance data. In this study, authors propose two nonparametric queue length estimation algorithms based on temporal analysis of vehicle interdistance fluctuations. The first algorithm identifies potential queue starts and ends using a moving average threshold method, while the second algorithm utilizes a weighted moving average to estimate interdistances for forward calculation of queue lengths. Comparative simulations showed that nonparametric methods matched the accuracy of parametric approaches based on constant time headway models, and in some cases outperformed traditional Bayesian multi-model estimation methods, especially when traffic conditions changed rapidly. Furthermore, authors found that the performance of nonparametric methods improved with increased frequency of vehicle speed measurements, and offered practical solutions for reducing computational costs and eliminating negative estimates. The study's findings provide a theoretical foundation for further development of cooperative adaptive cruise control systems that utilize queue length information. Authors suggest considering additional factors such as lane changes and priority systems to improve the practical applicability of the methods presented. The proposed algorithms are publicly available online at Bitbucket. With global positioning system data from 12 test drivers in the United States and Sweden, authors found that the estimated queue lengths were within 20 meters of actual values 90% of the time. The estimated queue lengths had a mean absolute error of 5 meters or less in 50% of the cases. The proposed methods require approximately 0.05 seconds of computational cost per data point, making them suitable for real-time applications. The study's findings are relevant to various cooperative adaptive cruise control systems that rely on global positioning system data from vehicle-to-infrastructure communications. Authors propose integrating the queue length estimation system into the controller module of the system architecture, and suggest future research directions including prioritization systems and cooperative adaptive cruise control systems in multi-lane scenarios. The study's limitations include the absence of vehicle-to-vehicle communication data, and the limited test driver population. The proposed methods assume that vehicle speed measurements exceed 10 km/h, and that vehicle speeds are measured at the same frequency as vehicle positions, which may not always be the case in real-world applications. The study's duration of 30 minutes may not be sufficient to evaluate the performance of the methods in scenarios with prolonged traffic conditions. We've developed a new strategy for resolving the Hamiltonian constraint, tailored for self-gravitating, relativistic fluids, and it forms the basis for a broader numerical relativity scheme that solves the full Einstein field equations simultaneously. This novel approach bypasses the conventional 3+1 split methodology and instead employs a conformal transformation to transform the Hamiltonian constraint into a nonlinear, second-order differential equation for the conformal factor, which is solved using an iterative method. Once determined, the conformal factor is used to calculate the other variables. This method differs from traditional approaches by treating the conformal factor non-dynamically and utilizing an advanced multigrid solver to solve the resulting nonlinear equation. Numerical tests, including a collapsing, charged dust ring and an interacting fluid system with a rotating shockwave, demonstrate the scheme's efficacy. These simulations show that our method yields similar results when compared to established methods, but with a substantial decrease in computational time required to complete simulations of identical duration. Specifically, a case involving a dust ring required the new method to complete 1500 timesteps in 20 hours, in contrast to the established method which took 10 hours to complete the same number of timesteps. This scheme's efficiency is attributed to the non-recursive solution of the Hamiltonian constraint and the use of a dynamic solver for the conformal factor. This method's effectiveness is particularly evident when simulating shockwave interactions with scattering off mass asymmetry, for which the new method allowed for the first time the simulation of a shockwave interacting with a dust ring up to 100 times smaller in mass, without the need to rescale the parameters. This capability was previously inaccessible due to the collapse of such small rings within the timescales simulated in this work. This new method's potential is further highlighted by the complex dynamics unveiled in the interaction of two shockwaves with charged dust distributions of different masses and sizes. This discovery suggests that antiferromagnetic anti-Perovskite materials may serve as ideal platforms for exploring anomalous thermal transport phenomena influenced by magnetic fields. sensors. By applying a genetic algorithm, our neural network achieved a notable
improvement, with a 30% reduction in mean squared error compared to standard
training methods. Utilizing a genetic algorithm enabled our self-sensing composite
to accurately detect various types of damage, with results showing a 25% error

cracks. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of a genetic algorithm in
training a neural network for damage detection in composites without the need

in resolving the distinction between actual damage signals and background noise.

We've developed an adaptable model based on the Lotka-Volterra system that simulates the intricate relationships between intelligent predators, preys, and their environment. By incorporating the concept of optimal control, this model allows our species to make informed decisions that maximize their own survival and prosperity, taking into account the current state of the ecosystem and any external costs associated with their actions. Through numerical computations, our Lotka-Volterra system reveals a stable coexistence between the intelligent species, as well as a fascinating "tragedy of the commons" effect where both species ultimately perish as a result of their individual efforts to prioritize their own self-interest. Furthermore, our research includes a Markov chain model that provides insight into the long-term outcomes of our Lotka-Volterra system, and also offers policy recommendations that could potentially lead to a harmonious coexistence between the species. Our study builds upon the existing works of Mallet-Pinou and of Huang, Liu, and Zhang, and our results complement the findings of Huang, Liu, and Zhang. Our Lotka-Volterra system can be applied to various real-world scenarios, such as managing fish populations or understanding the dynamics of competing plant species in an ecosystem. Our research was motivated by the desire to explore the complex interactions between self-interested species that are capable of adapting to their environment, and to investigate the potential consequences of these interactions on the stability of these ecosystems. Our model assumptions are reasonable given the current state of scientific knowledge, as there is limited research available on the dynamics of intelligent species in response to changing environmental conditions. Our Lotka-Volterra system can be extended to incorporate additional factors that influence the coexistence of species, such as random fluctuations within the ecosystem or the adoption of cooperative behavior. Our research includes a numerical computation of the long-term outcomes of our Lotka-Volterra system using a Euler method with a small time step of 0.001, and our results showed that the system converged to its steady-state within approximately 1000 time steps. Our Markov chain model was inspired by the research of Mallet-Pinou, and our policy recommendations are based on the strategy of maintaining the current population levels of both species until the outcomes of our Lotka-Volterra system become clear, at which point we can adjust our policies accordingly. Our Lotka-Volterra system can be applied to various self-similar ecosystems, such as coral reefs or forests, and our research provides policy insights for managing these ecosystems, particularly in the context of overfishing or deforestation.

This finding extends previous results by Horbe, Reid, and Shpall, who showed that specific $SL_2$ lattices have biautomatic properties. Consider a right-angled Artin group whose graph contains a subgraph whose vertex neighborhoods are all disconnected from each other. We demonstrate that this subgraph can be used to create a specific type of tree upon which the group acts, characterized by a unique vertex that isn't part of any orbit under the group's action. Additionally, this tree isn't linked to any other orbit, making it an isolated component. Moreover, when the group is infinite, this tree has a finite diameter and a limited number of components. Building on this discovery, we can further investigate the properties of a tree acted upon by a surface group that contains a specific subgraph, and we can determine the surface's topological characteristics in response. Moreover, we can determine the group's asymptotic cone and the characteristics of its link, and we can show that it isn't a ray, and its distal part isn't empty. Based on these findings, the problem of determining if the asymptotic cone of a surface group whose action on a tree contains a specific subgraph is a tree becomes solvable after the introduction of an additional assumption, and this assumption can be interpreted geometrically. Furthermore, this assumption holds true for a specific class of surface groups, and it provides a theoretical explanation for the non-tree structure observed in previous research. The main arguments used to arrive at these conclusions draw heavily from the insights gained from the study of group actions on trees by Gueritaud, Guiraud, Paulos, and Vitale. Many real-world networks, including collaborative systems and brain networks, evolve over time in response to external stimuli. These dynamic graphs have distinct structural properties that vary from their static counterparts, necessitating specialized machine learning models. Our proposed DECENNT model addresses this challenge by simultaneously predicting graph changes and encoding its current state, leveraging both historical network data and external influence factors. In contrast to traditional approaches that treat graph evolution as a sequential problem, DECENNT models graph changes as a stochastic differential equation, allowing it to capture nuanced temporal relationships and distinguish genuine network components from artifacts of sampling, even in sparse graphs. Our model's performance is demonstrated through numerical examples and brain network predictions, showing improved results compared to existing methods, particularly in tasks like graph classification and link prediction. DECENNT's unique capabilities are highlighted in experiments involving synthetic data and real-world brain networks, showcasing its ability to recover hidden network components and accurately predict brain connectivity from functional MRI scans. Our proposed model is valuable for analyzing complex networks that evolve over time and have vast potential for extension into more intricate applications. Our code is available at https://github.com/yingtong/DECENNT.

By applying sophisticated image processing techniques, our proposed system can accurately identify the direction particles are moving within biological samples such as swimming bacteria and moving cells. This distinction allows our algorithm to separate moving particles into three categories based on their speed: slow movers like cells, medium-speed movers like some bacteria, and fast movers like certain bacterial species. Our approach achieves this without relying on time-consuming frame-by-frame video analysis and produces consistent results across multiple sample images for both static and rapidly shot videos. Our experiments using both simulated and real images show our method's effectiveness and efficiency. Our software is designed to be user-friendly and can be utilized for monitoring particle movement patterns and velocities within biological samples by researchers in the life sciences community. Our program is particularly suited for identifying bacterial motility patterns and evaluating the efficacy of antibacterial agents in static and moving samples. Our approach provides a straightforward GUI for directing the image preprocessing steps, offers customizable settings for adjusting particle detection parameters, and includes graphical representations of particle movement velocity and direction. Our system also generates detailed statistical data about particle movements, including peak velocity values and the distribution of particle speeds. Our algorithm can be applied across various research areas that involve analyzing the movement of individual particles within biological samples, including the study of bacterial biofilms, the assessment of antibacterial agent efficacy, the monitoring of stem cell movement, and the analysis of yeast cell movements. Our software is available online for academic research purposes only and can be accessed at https://github.com/NeuralBIO group/MOP-VIDEOPROC. Our proposed approach is distinct from other particle tracking algorithms due to its ability to accurately determine the direction of particle movement, especially for particles moving in complex and curved paths, based on the analysis of video frames over time. Our algorithm significantly outperforms the conventional corner detection method, especially for particles moving in circular motions, and provides a clearer and more precise understanding of particle movements within biological samples. Our software has numerous applications in the life sciences community, including the study of bacterial motility patterns, the evaluation of antibacterial agent efficacy, the monitoring of stem cell movement, and the analysis of yeast cell movements. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments using both simulated and real images of various research samples, including images of bacterial biofilms, yeast cells, and stem cells. Our algorithm's efficiency and accuracy are further highlighted by the results of the 2D particle tracking challenge, where our method ranks among the top performers compared to other state-of-the-art algorithms. In the context of nested convex optimization, the Nested Neumann algorithm achieves optimal linear convergence rates when targeting narrow performance metrics, specifically when these metrics have a limited "inception depth". This paper builds upon this insight to develop a novel nested framework, tailored for optimization problems that involve multiple, interconnected performance metrics with distinct scales. By redefining the algorithm's target to focus on the underlying large-scale problem, the Nested Neumann framework is able to achieve a faster linear convergence rate, with a coefficient that is directly influenced by the difference in scales between the large and small problems. To illustrate the effectiveness of this approach, the paper presents a specific application of the nested framework to a scenario involving the optimization of a communication network in a specific context, prior to providing numerical results that demonstrate the benefits of using the Nested Neumann algorithm in this particular example.
