In recent years, Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have achieved outstanding performance in clustering and node classification tasks within spherical hyperbolic spaces. However, existing solutions have limitations when dealing with large-scale graphs due to their high computational costs. To break through this constraint, we propose a novel Lorentzian Graph Convolutional Network (LGCN), a method that generalizes graph convolution to Lorentzian space and introduces an efficient multi-layer Lorentzian GCN architecture. Compared to current state-of-the-art hyperbolic GCNs, LGCN significantly improves node feature representations with a substantial reduction in computational expenses. To evaluate the effectiveness of LGCN, we apply a standard GCN training procedure on various spherical and hyperbolic graph datasets, and our results show that LGCN outperforms existing hyperbolic GCNs by a notable margin in terms of classification accuracy. Moreover, LGCN achieves comparable performance to spherical GCNs on spherical datasets at a fraction of the computational cost. To further illustrate LGCN's efficiency, we conduct extensive experiments on large-scale hyperbolic graph datasets and find that LGCN reduces the computational burden by an order of magnitude compared to current solutions. To facilitate comprehensive research on graph learning within complex spaces, we open-source LGCN at https://github.com/zwang84/LGCN.

This note focuses on stability issues in inverse problems involving the one-way wave equation, a model often used to study seismic inversion methods. When measuring the velocity of a medium through surface measurements, small changes in velocity can result in significantly different images, making it essential to establish sharp bounds on which medium can produce a given data set, based on minimal information. To achieve this, Carriero, Colombardo, and Panabés adapted an approach by Choudour-Paounann and Shishakin to demonstrate that a Carleman estimate could be used to obtain a sharp observability inequality, effectively making the one-way wave equation an internally controlled system. This observation inequality serves as a critical component in establishing $H^{-1}$ regularity for the velocity coefficient when measuring through a single surface measurement. As a result, we are able to prove that a simple gradient method converges to the exact velocity in $C^1$ norm when measuring through a single surface measurement with full data. Furthermore, this regularity can be improved to $C^{1,\delta}$ when measuring through multiple surface measurements with partial data, for any $\delta > 0$. Ultimately, this regularity can be utilized to develop convergent iterative methods for a wide range of non-linear inversion problems, including the one we demonstrate with the Born approximation under partial data measurements. Ultimately, this can result in a velocity image with the desired level of smoothness. The Tsallis distribution has widespread applications in physics, yet its origins remain unclear, prompting us to re-examine its foundation. We present a social system analogy where individuals prioritize fairness over maximizing their personal gains, leading to Tsallis-like distribution patterns. By considering multiple scenarios and system sizes, we demonstrate how our simple model replicates distinctive features of the Tsallis distribution, offering a broader understanding of its utility across physical and biological domains. Our research indicates that Tsallis statistics are not exclusive to random processes, but can also arise from the interconnectedness of complex systems, particularly when fairness is valued over self-interest. We anticipate that our social framework will serve as a stepping stone for investigating other Tsallis-like phenomena observed in biological and physical systems. Our specific findings include not only the expected bell-shaped curve, but also explanations for negative skewness, bimodality, power-law behavior, and system size effects on the Tsallis exponent. We further demonstrate how our model can be used to interpret recent biophysical studies on the Tsallis distribution, shedding new light on the underlying mechanisms driving these patterns. Our parting remark is that the Tsallis distribution's status as a marker of complexity may sometimes be misleading, as it can arise from remarkably simple, self-consistent decision-making processes in individual system components. We hope our social system model will facilitate the re-examination of existing Tsallis distribution findings and encourage future researchers to consider alternative, non-random explanations for complex phenomena. We acknowledge that our model's limitations lie in its focus on uncorrelated systems and stress the importance of extending its principles to complex networks and interconnected systems. We also emphasize the critical role of fairness in our model and propose the term "fairness-induced Tsallis statistics" (FITS) to describe this specific phenomenon, distinguishing it from other physical and biological contexts that may give rise to Tsallis-like distributions. We suspect that the true essence of the Tsallis distribution lies in its relationship to the concept of fairness, rather than complexity or non-thermality. We propose that the Tsallis distribution should be viewed with caution, as it can arise from a wide range of distinct mechanisms, including, but not limited to, complex systems, time series, and biophysical phenomena. We believe that our research provides a compelling social system-based explanation for the widespread occurrence of the Tsallis distribution, suggesting that its utility may be, in part, a result of overfitting due to the limited number of its parameters. We anticipate that our findings will give rise to a broader understanding of the Tsallis distribution

In this note, we outline a method to analyze the degrees of freedom in linearized gravity theories by utilizing a $2\times2$ matrix representation of the linearized gravitational field equations. A change of variable allows us to express the mass term as a $2\times2$ matrix, whose degrees of freedom can be determined using the rank-one update decomposition of matrix variables. This approach enables us to identify the true degrees of freedom in linearized gravity theories with a mass term, specifically in $f(R)$ gravity and in theories with a specific combination of Ricci square and Ricci scalar terms. Unlike previous analyses, our method demonstrate that in $f(R)$ gravity, there are only two true degrees of freedom instead of three. Additionally, our investigation of the rank-one update decomposition reveals a distinct feature in the behavior of solutions in the context of the Einstein static universe. We also observe that in $f(R)$ gravity, the true degree of freedom that remains unfrozen at the initial stage $t=0$ is the one controlled by the mass term, whereas in the Einstein static universe scenario, the rank-one update decomposition leads to a vanishing Ricci square term. Our approach can be extended to analyze other gravity theories with a mass term. Our findings are validated through a comparative analysis with alternative approaches, including the Hamiltonian constraint and the Hamiltonian vector constraint, in the context of $f(R)$ gravity. Our method offers a distinct and complementary insight into the physics of these systems, revealing novel characteristics that were previously unobserved. A common analogy to explain negative temperature relies on a metaphor of "hot water" compared to a system at negative temperature, but we believe a more precise and instructive analogy would be to use a two-level system, similar to atomic energy levels.  In this case, we can create a theoretical model consisting of two interacting harmonic oscillators, one with a frequency twice that of the other, and calculate their joint temperature based on their energy distribution.  Our analysis shows that when we increase the energy of the system, the temperature can become negative, and to illustrate this concept visually, we created a three-dimensional plot of the system's energy versus the temperature of its components, with the understanding that the "higher" component actually represents the system's overall temperature, and the "lower" component represents the temperature of its individual parts.  Our results also indicate that the system's temperature becomes asymmetric during heat exchange, and in one scenario, where the system starts at negative temperature and is allowed to evolve over time, we plotted its temperature development in a 3D volume.  In this last example, we compared two scenarios, one where the system is allowed to interact with its environment, and another where it is isolated, and we observed that the system will always return to a state of positive temperature when it is allowed to interact with its environment, and that the direction of this return is asymmetrical.  In the closing section, we discuss our results in the context of previous research, and we believe that our two-level system model provides a clear and intuitive visual representation of the concept of negative temperature.  Our calculations also align with the findings of other researchers who used different methods, and we hope that our results will aid in the public's understanding of this phenomenon.  Our model has the added benefit of being easily extensible to more complex systems of multiple levels, and we have made our code available online for the benefit of the scientific community. Researchers are utilizing ultrafast optical excitations to manipulate the electronic properties of transition metal oxides in unique ways, and are now investigating these phenomena in $L_1$-edge experiments on Sr$_2$TaO$_5$ film. The results show that optical excitations can switch the effective spin-orbit coupling, influence the energy gaps between different electronic levels, and lead to the formation of unusual electronic states, lasting microns, which can be controlled by varying the intensity of the excitation. The findings are well-explained by theoretical models and highlight the potential for creating and controlling unique electronic conditions in transition metal oxides using ultrafast optical stimuli. The potential applications of this discovery include developing novel materials with unique electronic properties and creating devices with unique functionality, operating at microwave frequencies, with a small footprint. Through the manipulation of hidden codes, generative models can provide insights into the underlying representations of images. In the context of medical imaging, this approach can help explore the representations of diseases and injuries in images by generating synthetic data. Our study utilizes the AAAI medical challenge dataset, which comprises CT scans with markers or lesions added at unknown locations, making it an ideal choice for this research. By training an ATAE encoder-extractor using a standard latent code manipulation technique, our results show that the model effectively predicts the represented location, size, and shape of the added pathologies from synthetic scans. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the hidden code corresponds to a spherical coordinate system, with the radius representing the severity of the represented condition, the colatitude indicating the organ location, and the longitude reflecting the specific location within an organ. Our approach can be applied to other medical datasets featuring artificially introduced abnormalities. In essence, this research demonstrates the capability of generative models to elicit explicit understanding of medical image representations by code manipulation, offering a promising non-intrusive approach for exploring high-dimensional medical data. Our code has been made available online at the specified repository. System requirements for running the code include Python 3.8, PyTorch 1.8, and BERT 1.1.3. Future directions involve utilizing this approach for quantitative assessment of lesion detection algorithms and developing models that can handle multiple introduced pathologies. ViDaExpert is an interactive visualization and dimensionality reduction tool designed to facilitate the exploration of high-dimensional data. It offers a straightforward GUI for selecting the most relevant data features, as well as two main visualization modes: a scatter plot that can be panned, zoomed, and colored based on different features, and a t-SNE representation of the data. The latter view enables the user to mark clusters of interest, which are then highlighted in the scatter plot. ViDaExpert was created to complement the special issue on evolutionary algorithms by providing researchers with an accessible means to visually examine large datasets. The tool is available online at the address indicated in the text. 

To facilitate the assessment of ViDaExpert's effectiveness, the accompanying dataset comprises performance metrics from 24 benchmark functions, each tested with 10 different problem sizes, resulting in a total of 240 data points. These results are preloaded into the tool, which the authors invite readers to explore with ViDaExpert. 

It is worth noting that ViDaExpert can be used for visualizing any high-dimensional dataset, not just the specific dataset considered in this study. The tool's source code is also included for developers interested in modifying its features or integrating its functionality into other projects. 

In the appendix, the authors present a detailed evaluation of alternative visualization techniques, including the application of various distance metrics to measure the similarity between data clusters, as well as an examination of the effects of different dimensionality reduction methods on the t-SNE views generated by ViDaExpert. 

In the process, the authors discovered several notable issues with existing solutions, including the fact that popular t-SNE implementations cannot handle sparse matrices, leading them to release a new version of the t-SNE code that can do so. This updated code is also made available as part of the supplementary materials. 

In the final section of the appendix, the authors conduct a set of manual cluster assessments to evaluate the effectiveness of ViDaExpert in identifying meaningful data clusters, particularly in the context of the specific dataset considered in this study, which comprises performance metrics from 24 benchmark functions tested with varying problem sizes, resulting in a total of 240 data points. 

To perform the assessment, the authors employed ViDaExpert to generate a t-SNE representation of the data, which they then manually examined to identify clusters of interest, which they subsequently validated by re-running the evolutionary algorithms with different problem sizes and examining the resulting data points in the t-SNE space.
